Summary

Phainon was too young, too reckless, and too in love with the idea of saving everyone but himself. So when his kingdom decided to send his childhood friend as a peace offering to the tyrant king of Kremnos, Phainon did what no one expected.

He took her place.

Wrapped in gown and secrets, he expected humiliation or death. What he didn’t expect was to stand face to face with Mydeimos, the feared immortal king… who looked strangely familiar.

What started as a desperate bluff turns into something far more complicated. Between court politics, old wounds, and strange sparks neither of them dare name, Phainon finds himself caught in a situation that he had never imagined.

But hearts can be reckless. Promise is soul-binding.

And sometimes, the smallest choice rewrites everything.

chapters.title: The Mysterious Kitty Cat
chapters.html:
The capital city of Aedes Elysia was more like a rural town but hummed with a quiet warmth. Golden wheat fields swayed lazily in the breeze, brushing against the low stone walls like waves on a gentle tide. Further off, the sea whispered against a wooden dock that stretched over salt-licked rocks, planks warped and sun-bleached from years of sun and storm. A windmill turned with steady grace near the crest of the hill, its broad sails casting fleeting shadows over the autumn-dyed trees that clustered around the stone buildings.


And somewhere in that golden sprawl of wind and wheat and saltwater laughter, a boy ran barefoot with a grin as wide as the horizon.


Phainon.


Twelve years old and all sunshine. His hair, pale as frost in moonlight, flared like a silver flame as he darted between the tall stalks, arms stretched like wings. The wind tangled through it, tugging at the hem of his faded tunic. His eyes, bright, unclouded blue, reflected the sky above and the sea below, two twin oceans full of curiosity and mischief.


He’d abandoned his sandals hours ago, leaving them dangling off the edge of a half-finished fence. The soles of his feet were darkened with dust and grain chaff, but he moved like he didn’t feel it, like the earth knew him and softened just for his passing. Occasionally, he’d leap to snatch at the floating dandelion seeds drifting in the air, laughing when they slipped through his fingers and danced out of reach.


From the distance came the low creak of wood as he clambered up a leaning tree near the old mill. It wasn’t even the tallest one in the grove, but it was his favorite. The branches bent just right for climbing, the bark rough enough to scrape his palms without drawing blood. He perched there like a prince in a tower, legs swinging, one hand shading his eyes as he scanned the coast.


His eyes gleamed as he spotted the glint of silver scales near the river bend. Phainon scrambled down in a tumble of leaves and laughter, bolting toward the water. It wasn’t far. The river fed into the sea just beyond the wheat fields, and the wooden dock curved alongside it like a spine of an old sea creature. He barely paused when he reached it, throwing off his overshirt and charging into the shallows with a delighted shout.


The water wasn’t warm, but he didn’t care. The thrill of the hunt burned hot in his chest. He crouched low, wading deeper with careful steps. His fingers were spread like claws, ready to strike. The fish flitted away, darting just out of reach. But he was patient. He’d done this dozens of times—learned the rhythm of the stream, the patterns of the light. A sharp splash, and his hands closed around a thrashing body, slippery and alive.


“Gotcha!”


He lifted it triumphantly, droplets spraying into the air like little sparks of light. For a second, the setting sun caught the arc of water and turned it gold.


Phainon grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.


Dripping wet and still clutching his prize, he made his way back to the dock, tossing the fish into a wooden bucket he’d left there earlier.


After he caught two more fishes, he made the makeshift grill, built it from dry sticks, pine cones, and a few flat stones arranged into a crude pit. He had learned to make after too many failed attempts involving charred fish and burned fingers. Now, the skewered fishes rested neatly on two branches propped over the flames, skin blistering to a crisp, fat hissing where it dripped. Smoke rose in soft tendrils, drifting lazily into the autumn air, mingling with the scent of the sea and the faint tang of scorched pinecone. Phainon proudly rotating the skewers, humming softly.


He was still damp. His silvery-blue hair stuck up in every direction from drying haphazardly in the wind, and his cheeks were flushed with satisfaction. Until suddenly,


Rustle.


He stiffened.


Something had moved in the bushes. Just behind the cluster of wild ginkgo trees near the dock.


Phainon narrowed his eyes toward the noise. Maybe it was a fox again. Or a cat. Hopefully not the goat from the baker’s house. Last time, it ran off with his whole basket of bread.


Carefully, he set the half-cooked fishes aside and crept toward the undergrowth, brushing leaves aside with quiet fingers. “Come on out, I heard you…”


The branches parted, and he froze.


There, crouched low in the shadows, was a child.


Delicate features framed by unruly blond hair, skin was pale but dusted with fine dirt, and eyes, those eyes, blazing like molten gold. Spiraling across the figure’s arms and collar were vivid red markings, shaped like whorls of flame dancing along the skin. The ragged tunic and thin frame barely concealed the ethereal presence.


Phainon stared, wide-eyed. "Whoa... you're really pretty."


The child blinked, startled.


“Are you… lost, young miss?" Phainon said, somehow tried to sound like a dependable older man.


But somehow, he made the pretty visage marred by a deep scowl.


“I’m not a girl.”


Phainon’s face went scarlet. “Oh, uh, oops? I mean, sorry! It’s just, you’re really...like, your face is all… you know, shiny and your hair’s all... fluffy.”


The boy’s brows furrowed even more. He shifted as if to run.


“Wait! Don’t go!” Phainon stepped forward quickly, arms raised in harmless surrender. “I didn’t mean to offend you or anything. Just, are you hungry?”


The boy hesitated, head tilted in a way that reminded Phainon of a wary animal. His lips parted.


"No, I..."


But a loud rumble echoed from his stomach.


They both froze.


The boy’s face turned bright red.


Phainon's eyes dilated and then burst into laughter. Not mocking, but bright and delighted. He grinned wide, a tooth missing on the upper right. “I knew it.”


He ran back to the fire, grabbed the best-looking fish skewer, and returned to the bushes. The boy hadn’t moved, just stood there stiffly, fists clenched at his sides, like pride was keeping him rooted even though his belly had other plans.


Phainon extended the fish. “Here. You can have it. I caught it with my own hands. It’s amazing. Or maybe terrible. But it smells good, right?”


The boy looked at the offering like it was some kind of trap.


“It’s not poisoned,” Phainon added quickly. “If it was, I’d be dead already. Or at least hiccupping funny.”


No reaction. But those golden eyes flicked to the fish again. Hunger made his fingers twitch.


After another moment, the boy stepped forward slowly. Gingerly, he took the skewer from Phainon’s hand, careful not to touch anything else. He didn’t say thanks. Just stared at the fish like it was the first real food he’d seen in days.


“You can sit, if you want,” Phainon offered, plopping back onto the ground without waiting. “The fire’s warm. And I won’t ask if you’re secretly a forest elf. Even though you do look kind of magical.”


That earned a side-eye glare, but he finally settled on the spot Phainon offered.


Phainon just grinned wider. The sun dipped lower in the sky, casting their small circle in a pool of amber light.


He then plopped down beside the quiet boy without hesitation, holding a fish in one hand. The boy sat a little stiffly, clutching his skewer close like it might disappear. He didn’t say a word. Didn’t look directly at Phainon either, not unless he thought he wasn’t being watched.


But Phainon talked anyway.


He talked about everything. About how he once slipped on a wet dock and fell into the sea, about how Old Lady down the windmild swore her goose laid golden eggs (it didn’t), about the time he tried to ride a wild goat and got bucked straight into a haystack. His words spilled out in excited bursts, all bright and unfiltered, accompanied by wild hand gestures and animated expressions.


“And then, I swear this happened, there was this big fish, like this big,” he spread his arms wide, nearly slapping the boy, “and it jumped out of the bucket and started flopping away! I chased it all the way to the mill, and guess what? It got stuck between the floorboards! I had to pry it out with a broom handle!”


The boy didn’t laugh.


He sat there, nibbling quietly on the fish, casting the occasional glance from behind the curtain of messy blond hair. When Phainon caught him staring, he’d look away fast, ears burning.


Phainon grinned every time. He didn’t point it out. Just kept talking, letting his voice fill the silence between them like sunlight creeping through the clouds.


“You don’t talk much, huh..,” he said after a brief pause to chew. “You can just listen. My mom says I talk enough for two people anyway.”


The boy didn’t reply, but his shoulders relaxed just a little.


The light grew softer, slipping into that golden hush that always came before night. Crickets began their song somewhere beyond the wheat, and the windmill’s creak blended into the rhythm of the waves. Phainon leaned back on his hands, chewing the last bite of his fish, utterly content. It didn’t even matter that he’d done most of the talking, somehow, the silence felt full instead of empty.


Finally, the boy stood. His hand lingered at his side like he wasn’t sure what to do with it. He turned toward the trees again, ready to vanish back into whatever mysterious place he’d come from.


Phainon stood too, brushing crumbs from his lap. “Hey.”


The boy paused.


“I’ll be here again tomorrow,” Phainon said. “Same place. I’ll catch more fish. Or, maybe I’ll bring fruit. You can come back if you want.”


The boy didn’t say anything. But as he walked away, just before the shadows swallowed him, he looked back.


Just once.


Then he dashed off, quiet and quick as a whisper between trees.


Phainon came back the next day.


And the day after that.


And the next.


He brought fish, of course, his pride and specialty. Then, he also started to bring bread rolls he snuck from the bakery when the old man wasn’t looking, fruits from a neighbor’s garden (with permission, mostly), and once, a suspiciously large stash of nuts in cloth pouch.


Each day, at nearly the same time, the boy showed up.


He never came out of his hiding spot until Phainon was already there, fire crackling, food set out like an offering. He then would slip out of the bushes like a shadow, always barefoot, always silent at first. Phainon grinned at him, every time, like he was a miracle.


And each time, they sat together, shoulder to shoulder or side by side. Sharing food, watching the waves. Phainon talked, about his dreams, the weird things he read, the dumb things he did. And the boy listened. Quietly.


One afternoon, as Phainon told the dramatic tale of the time he got stuck in the hayloft trying to rescue a cat that turned out to be a hat, the boy snorted. A real sound.


Phainon turned, eyes wide. “Did you just laugh?!”


“No."


“You did! You totally did!” Phainon leaned closer, grinning so hard his cheeks hurt. “Admit it! That was a laugh!”


“It was a breath.”


“Oh, a breath,” Phainon echoed mockingly, clutching his chest like he was wounded. “I breathed once when I fell into the river and almost drowned. So I get it. Laughing. Breathing. Totally the same thing.”


The boy didn’t answer.


But he did smile. Just a little. Barely there.


They started playing, too.


Tag in the tall wheat, where the grain brushed against their arms and made every movement feel like a secret. Sometimes they climbed trees or skipped stones by the dock, and once, Phainon convinced the boy to help him build a floating raft. It didn’t float. It sank dramatically, but they laughed until they cried, or rather, Phainon laughed until he cried, while the boy just stood there looked at the sad raft with deep frown, pondering. On the next day, the boy insisted they try it again and they managed to make a proper one, the raft floated away with some chesnuts on top.


And when they heard voices, farmers, travelers, anyone passing nearby, the boy would freeze. He always disappeared behind the nearest bush or tree, face stiff, golden eyes narrowed. Phainon learned to stop asking questions. Instead, he started helping.


“Quick!” he’d hiss, grabbing the boy’s hand and ducking behind the rocks. “Let's play hide and seek!”


“...Who will be the finder if we both hide?” the boy muttered once.


“Everyone else! We're hiding together!"


Another time, Phainon pushed the boy down the haystacks, hovering above him. “Okay, stay still. Pretend you're a cat.”


“What.” The boy's visage brightened slightly even with the raised eyebrows.


“A really sneaky cat. You're a cat now.”


The boy stared.


“You gotta commit to the act,” Phainon whispered, chewing on a piece of straw. “Meow with dignity... Hm?” He bent lower, sniffing. "You smell like flower..."


The boy shoved him away.


Phainon yelped, exaggerated, and flopped over dramatically into the hay. The boy didn’t help him up, but he sat beside him afterward, picking stray stalks from his sleeves.


Days after days, they spent it together yet Phainon still hadn't learn his name. He tried to ask for a name a few more times. Once, he asked outright. Another time, he tried to guess.


“Is it… Flamey? Because of your cool tattoos?”


Silence.


“Okay. What about Blaze? Or Ember? Ooh, what if it’s something epic like ‘Ashes of the Dying Sun’?”


The boy gave him a judging gaze..


Eventually, Phainon stopped asking.


He just started calling him “you,” or “hey,” or on particularly smug days, “Mysterious Kitty Cat” or "Cute fairy". Those earned a groan. A small one, painful even. But still, a reaction.


By now, the space beneath the golden trees felt like their own little world. A patch of earth untouched by time, where smoke curled gently in the air and laughter mingled with the rustle of wheat.


Phainon didn’t know who the boy was. Where he came from. Why he never gave his name. But the time they spent was so precious that he didn't even care anymore. All he wanted was just to feed the 'stray kitten' and maybe, made him smile, if he was lucky.


The fire crackled softly in the quiet of the late afternoon, but the usual rhythm was off.


Phainon noticed it the moment the boy arrived.


He came the same way he always did, slipping through like a shadow, barefoot and silent, but there was no glint of wonder in his golden eyes, no half-hidden smirk when he saw the fish already grilling. His posture was tight, shoulders drawn up like he was trying to disappear into himself, and he didn’t reach for the food at all.


Phainon didn’t say anything.


He just scooted over on the rock they always shared and sat beside him, legs swinging just short of the dirt. The fire flickered between them, casting long, warm shadows. Crickets chirped lazily from somewhere in the grass. Overhead, gulls circled the coastline like drifting bits of cloud.


The boy hunched forward, arms loosely wrapped around his knees.


Then his hand came up to his face.


First one. Then the other.


He rubbed his eyes, slowly, firmly. As if to wipe something away. As if to stop something from falling. He made no sound, but his breath came in shaky little pulls, just barely visible.


Still, Phainon didn’t speak.


He just leaned sideways, carefully, and wrapped both arms around the boy’s smaller frame. A gentle, quiet hug. No teasing, no jokes. Just warmth. Just pressure.


The boy tensed for a moment. His hands stayed at his face.


Then slowly, slowly, he lowered them and clung back.


He didn’t sob. He didn’t sniffle. But he held on tightly, as if he might fall apart if he let go too soon.


Phainon rested his chin lightly on the boy’s shoulder, one hand moving in slow, steady circles over his back.


Neither of them said a word.


Eventually, the boy released him. Not abruptly, just carefully, like he wasn’t quite ready but didn’t want to overstay the moment. Phainon leaned back, hands still in his lap, and offered a crooked smile.


He reached for the cloth-wrapped bundle beside the fire and pulled out a wooden cup, filled nearly to the brim with deep red juice. He held it out wordlessly.


The boy took it.


He sipped once, then paused. His eyes narrowed slightly, thoughtfully, not in distaste. Then he looked down at the cup and muttered, “...It’s good. But it’s better with milk.”


Phainon blinked. “What?”


The boy glanced at him, then down again. “Pomegranate juice. It’s better with goat milk.”


“Eugh,” Phainon made a face. “Is that even delicious?”


The boy nodded once, still not looking at him. “And cheese. Salty ones. It’s so good.”


Phainon furrowed his eyebrows, tilting his head like a confused puppy. “That sounds weird. Like. Really weird.”


The boy shrugged. “Don't judge my taste when you chew on hay.”


“Yeah, okay, good point.”


They sat like that for a long while, watching the flames shrink and stretch with the wind. The sky overhead melted from amber to soft indigo, and the scent of burning wood clung to their sleeves.


Phainon didn’t fill the silence with stories this time. He just sat with him. And the boy scooted closer, leaning on him. Phainon was surprised but he stayed still, placing his head against the golden strands. Phainon's hand soon found the other, and they held hands until the night fell.

The wind was gentle that morning, tugging at the tips of the wheat like a sleepy sigh. The sky was already bright, clouds soft and pale, and gulls were wheeling low over the shoreline. Phainon bounded over the ridge with a picnic bundle slung under one arm and a victorious grin on his face, his silver-blue hair practically glowing in the sun.


The boy was already there.


Waiting by their usual tree, arms crossed, golden eyes fixed on the horizon like he’d been standing there for a while. His expression didn’t change much when he saw Phainon, but maybe his shoulders eased a little.


Phainon jogged the rest of the way, winded but beaming. “You’re early! I brought, like, everything. Fish, bread, even the pomegranate juice with milk like you said! Don't ask how I got the milk.”


But the boy didn’t reach for the food.


“I’m leaving,” he said simply.


Phainon blinked. “Huh? Where?”


“Somewhere far,” the boy answered, his voice barely above whisper but thick with conviction.


"How far?"


"Really, far..."


Phainon’s grin faltered in each exchange. “Will you come back?”


There was no answer.


And that silence said everything.


He stared for a second, then slowly set down his bundle without unwrapping it. “Then take this. It’s for the road. It’s got a lot, so you better eat all of it or I’ll be mad.”


The boy hesitated, then nodded. “Thank you.”


"So, you can say thank you?" Phainon teased, the boy only looked away sheepishly.


Phainon then scratched his head, then formed a bashful laugh. “Hey… can I ask you to do one thing before you go?”


The boy looked suspicious but nodded once, brows slightly furrowed.


Phainon pointed at him. “Close your eyes.”


“What?”


“Just do it! I’m not gonna throw fish at you or anything.”


The boy rolled his eyes and, after a second, closed them. Arms loose at his sides, lashes fluttered and rested on his cheeks, just waiting.


Phainon stepped forward then leaned in and pressed a quick, feather-light kiss to his lips.


The boy flinched and stumbled back like he'd been struck by lightning.


He tripped over a root and landed in the grass with a soft oof, eyes wide as saucers and face redder than a ripe tomato. “W, What was that for?!”


Phainon burst into laughter. “The tree, duh! People say it’s a magical tree. If you kiss someone under it, you’re destined lovers!”


“L, lover?! I’m a boy!” the kid shouted, scandalized, hands over his mouth like Phainon had cursed him.


“I know that!” Phainon said proudly, plopping down beside him. “You’re a boy, and you’re pretty, and I like you so much. Even if you're actually a goat, I still like you so much!”


The boy spluttered, still pink in the face.


Phainon leaned in again, crouching with all the drama of a prince kneeling before a princess, except the grass clung to his knees and he had dirt smudges on his cheeks.


“Listen, kitty,” he said, taking the boy’s hand gently. “We have to meet again. Okay? Next year. Or two years. Or hundred. I don’t care how long, it doesn’t matter. Just come back here someday.”


The boy looked at him, still flustered but managed to respond. “...I don’t want to make a promise I might break.”


Phainon smiled like  sunlight poured into a grin. “That’s okay. Don't promise me anything. Just remember that there's me waiting for you here so you have to stay safe and you must come back to see me.”


Then, still holding the boy’s hand, he leaned in again, slower this time.


The boy didn’t pull away.


It was just a peck, like before. Barely there. A brush of lips between children too young to understand what they were doing, but old enough to feel something shift, something quietly important.


When they parted, the boy looked down, his face flushed so red.


"You're so cute." Phainon grinned, ruffling the blond hair which soon earned a light slap.


"Stop that..." The boy stood up, adjusted the picnic bundle in his arms, gaze fixed ahead toward the sunlit path winding into the wheat. He took a step forward, then another,, shoulders squared like he’d already braced himself to disappear.


"I'm going."


"Mhm! See you someday!"


Phainon stood behind him, trying not to frown too much, hands deep in his pockets. He kicked at a pebble, watching it skitter.


But just as the boy reached the edge of the clearing, he stopped.


He turned around.


Phainon perked up instantly, bright-eyed. “Forget something?”


The boy hesitated then crossed the distance back in quick, soundless steps.


Before Phainon could say anything else, the boy leaned in, stood on his toes—and kissed him on the cheek.


Warm. Quick. And gone like the wind.


Phainon froze, mouth parted, cheeks slowly catching fire.


Then the boy stepped back, the faintest flicker of a smile pulling at his lips.


“I’ll be back,” he said softly.


And with that, he turned and ran, blond hair catching the sun, the bundle swinging in his grasp, bare feet kicking up little clouds of dust as he disappeared into the golden sea of wheat.


Phainon stood completely still.


Then, “AAAAA!!” he squealed, clutching his face, spinning in a circle like the wind-up toy he’d once broken open to see how it worked. “HE KISSED ME!!"


He dropped to the ground, rolled once in the grass, arms flailing, laughter echoed through the clearing, giddy and wild and entirely his own. 


And that was the last time he ever saw him.


Even so, Phainon kept coming back to their spot.


With fish. With stories. With juice and bread and new scars from adventures no one else would believe. Sometimes he laughed to himself, sometimes he sat in silence. Sometimes, he would turn to the empty spot beside him and say, “You’re sooo late.”


But he never stopped waiting.

chapters.title: Sacrificial Bride
chapters.html:
Not long after that soft goodbye beneath the tree, the world changed.

The boy never returned.

And Amphoreus forgot how peace had once tasted.

No one truly remembered how the war began, only that it had always seemed just over the horizon. Whispers of border skirmishes, assassinated envoys, bandits ran wild. Some whispered it was an ancient blood feud, a wound left festering between kingdoms too proud to bow. Others blamed lost treaties, promises carved in wax and parchment that crumbled with time and ambition. But those names, those reasons, had long since turned to ash. Buried beneath the rubble of cities, beneath the roots of burned forests, beneath the silence left by the dead.

What remained was ruin.

Amphoreus, once a sprawling land of kingdoms, forests, and flowing trade, became a field of fire. Wheat fields turned to kindling. The borders had become scars, the rivers choked with old blood. Forests burned until only black root and cinder remained. Roads, once used for travel and stories, now led to graveyards.

And through that smoke, one name rose like thunder crashing against mountainsides:

Kremnos.

It towered on high, carved into the stone cliffs like it had clawed itself up from the bones of the world. A spiral of bridges and towers, walls built not to protect but to crush. The city gleamed silver and gold, cruel and magnificent, like a blade unsheathed forever.

The Kremnoan banner didn’t flutter, it ripped through the wind. A sun-eater majestic lion, unfurling like a declaration of war.

Its people were carved in the same image. Forged for war, raised in its heat. In Kremnos, strength was not celebrated, it was demanded. Children were taught to wield blades before they could properly speak. Weakness was not scorned, it was erased. 

Glory wasn’t something inherited. It was carved, blood-soaked, seized in the clash of steel. Those who returned from the battlefield in shame were considered less than dead. To fall was acceptable. To survive without achievement was not. Mercy was an old myth. Compassion was a foreign tongue for many.

One by one, the other kingdoms of Amphoreus crumbled beneath their march.

Force fell to strategy. Strategy fell to brutality. Castles bowed. Forests bled. The stars themselves seemed to dim under Kremnos’s shadow.

And so, the world bent.

The war didn’t end. It simply grew quiet under Kremnos’s heel.

For years, Amphoreus lived in fear. Fear of Kremnos, fear of the man who ruled it with bloodstained hands and a wrathful heart: King Eurypon.

He was not just a tyrant. He was the monster people tried not to name directly. He demanded impossible taxes from neighboring states and, when they could not pay, reduced them to vassal nations, obedient in name, broken in spirit. He expanded Kremnos’s reach through brutality, not politics. While others fought to protect, the Kremnoans fought to prove they had the right to exist. They embraced death as something noble, not something to fear, the violence was something they naturally craved. Thus, Kremnos had never taste defeat.

Between the terror, rumors began to spread.

They came in whispers at first, like wind under doors: that Eurypon was searching for someone. Desperate. Unrelenting.

It was said he had once loved a son.

The boy had been born under a rare moon, radiant, golden-eyed, a child said to bear a soul too strong for his age. But a prophecy followed on the dear Prince's tenth birthday. One that told of ruin at the child’s hand. Ruin not of kingdoms, but of Eurypon himself. And so, in fear or madness, or both, the king tried to kill his own flesh and blood. Some whispered that Eurypon had been cursed, that some ancient magic had twisted his mind. Others believed it was no curse, only his nature, finally unbound.

Alas, he was failed. The boy disappeared before his blade was unseathed. Eurypon turned on his own queen. Gorgo, beloved by her people, sharp as frost and brave as war. He accused her of treason, of hiding the child. And when she would not confess, he executed his love of his life with his own hands.

Kremnos fell into deeper violence after that.

He searched for years. Across mountains, through cities razed to the ground, through sacred temples and forsaken wastelands. Always looking. Always destroying. All for the chance to kill a boy who may or may not still live.

But fate is not so easily outrun.

And when Eurypon was finally slain, it was by the very son he had tried to erase.

Mydeimos.

He returned not as a child, but as a storm. Taller than any memory dared imagine, golden eyes fierce, red markings etched like fire across his skin. He bore his mother’s spear—Gorgo’s Spear, a weapon forged for war and vengeance alike and with it, he struck down the tyrant king in the heart of Kremnos itself.

Some say the earth shook when Eurypon fell. That the golden sword monument cracked at its base. That the torches along the terraces dimmed, just for a moment, in awe.

The people did not cheer. Not openly. Fear still clung to their bones like frost. They had been ruled by blood too long to trust change.

Still, their eyes turned to the young king with dread.

He was the son of Eurypon, after all. Born of cruelty, raised by vengeance. And worse, there were whispers that he could not be killed. That Mydeimos’s body was forged beyond steel by his mother's prayers, that no blade could pierce him, no fire could touch him. That he bore not just strength, but immortality.

Moreover, the fall of Eurypon had left a void, and the bloodthirst of Kremnos ran deep. They waited for him to lead the next conquest. To finish what his father began.

They expected him to drown Amphoreus in war once more.

But Mydeimos chose differently.

Instead of raising another army, he gave them an arena.

A colosseum of iron and marble, white as bone and wide as pride. It stood at the center of Kremnos like a declaration of purpose. No longer would soldiers march to burn the world. Now, they would fight here. Blade against blade. Roar against roar. Strength would still be honored but without turning cities to ash.

The battles were brutal. The blood was real. But they gave Kremnos what it needed: release.

The hunger for violence was fed on sand and stone. The craving for dominance was dressed in ritual and rules. And slowly, barely, the rest of Amphoreus began to breathe.

Not in peace. Not yet.

The other kingdoms watched the Young King carefully, like archers with arrows notched. They offered alliances, trinkets dressed as tribute. They tried to claim him, to bend the legend to their banners.

Gilded gifts came first. Wagons of silver, warhorses draped in velvet, masks carved from obsidian. And when gold failed, they offered something else:

Marriage.

Princes and princesses draped in silk, each more polished than the last. Each one with a practiced smile and a promise tucked into their voice.

Mydeimos refused them all.

Not because he was proud. Not because he was cruel.

He simply didn’t care.

He had no time for games played with lace and lies. His days were full; overseeing the colosseum, training the elite guard, keeping Kremnos from tearing itself apart from the inside. His rule was not easy. He did not rule by fear, but by force of will. By action.

They called him cold. They called him divine. Some called him broken. But no one dared call him weak because no one could ever beat him, even when the throne was offered as the prize and he was ambushed by many at once.

Mydeimos was the indestructible monster.

He didn’t need a throne to be powerful.

And he didn’t need anyone to tell him what to do with it.

Meanwhile, Aedes Elysiae had always been a small kingdom of sunlight and neutrality.

Tucked between hills and sea, the valley had escaped conquest not through strength, but by sheer circumstance. Its borders cradled by cliffs, its heartland hidden behind wind-woven wheat fields and forests heavy with herbs and wildflowers. It was not the kind of place generals bothered to invade. There were no fortresses here, no ancient weapons sealed beneath the earth, no bloodlines of kings who claimed divine right. Only farmers. Shepherds. Herbalists. People who believed the rain more than they believed in steel.

Their weapons were hoes. Their armor were sun hats.

Even their songs were soft.

And in a world built on war, such softness was not safety, it was merely a delay.

Aedes Elysiae had no remarkable military. No cavalry to ride to its defense, no ancient magic to call down storms. When hungrier kingdoms turned their gaze eastward, they didn’t come with fire, they came with ink. Contracts instead of catapults. Treaties wrapped in velvet, with promises that shimmered on the surface like gold and rotted beneath like spoiled fruit.

The last of those treaties was signed under King Eurypon’s rule.

It was a cruel thing. Kremnos did not ask for loyalty, only payment. Every harvest season, Aedes Elysiae was to send five cartloads of vegetables, barrels of honey, sacks of grain measured to the ounce. It was a small price for peace, they were told. A shield carved from bread instead of bone.

But that kind of peace, like the rain, couldn't be summoned on command.

And that year, the skies dried up. The rivers ran sluggish. The soil grew tired, brittle. Fields that once bent heavy with grain now stood cracked and empty. The roots of every herb twisted in thirst. Wild bees died by the thousands. Half the harvest failed before it even began.

The council sent letters, apologies, updates, appeals.

Kremnos replied not with cavalry, but a single scroll bearing the seal of the tyrant, delivered by a grim-faced courier on a red horse:

"Fail once more, and Kremnos will take what is owed. Not in crops. In blood."

The meaning was clear.

There would be no second appeal. No room for mercy. Kremnos had no need for weak allies. It would feed its own hunger, one way or another.

Panic broke through the valley like wildfire.

The fields could not be coaxed to yield what wasn’t there. The sun would not change its course for frightened men. The land moved at its own pace. But fear moved quicker.

And in that fear, a single voice rose.

Theo, the oldest among them. A former envoy. He had lived through three monarchs, one failed siege, and the signing of every trade agreement Aedes Elysiae had ever clung to. His hands shook with age, but his words did not.

“The Young King may be cruel,” he said, seated beneath the council’s carved tree of judgment, “but he is not senseless.”

They all looked to him. Even the new magistrates who scoffed at his old ways paused to listen.

He proposed a gamble.

If they could not offer coin, or crops, they would offer Cyrene.

She was not just their princess. She was the valley’s light, adored by children, revered by healers, followed by songbirds and strays alike. She had a calmness about her that soothed horses and made wolves blink as if waking from a dream. When she walked the fields, even birds hovered longer around her sleeves. Gentle, serene, and untouched by pride.

She was not a warrior.

But she had her own charm.

And in a world full of brutality, gentleness itself could be terrifying.

The council agreed. Not because they believed the idea was good, but because they had no other way out.

And Cyrene, she did not protest.

She bowed her head when the council spoke. She did not cry, nor rage. But those who knew her best saw the change. Saw the silence behind her smile. The way she folded her cloak one last time like she didn’t mean to ever wear it again.

She understood what she had become.

Not a gift. Not a bride. Not even a person.

She was a prayer carved in soft flesh. A gamble made in desperation. And every action in front of the ruthless king, no matter how small, might become the reason of her homeland's demise.

She was their last hope, their last defense.

The wheels of the carriage creaked over uneven stone, a slow, aching rhythm beneath the rising tension inside. Outside the window, the lush hills of Aedes Elysiae had long since receded into the haze of memory, replaced by harsher earth and wind-scoured cliffs. The green had faded to gray. The scent of wild thyme and grain had given way to the cold tang of stone.

In the distance, rising like a clenched fist against the pale sky, stood Kremnos.

A city that did not welcome. A monument to conquest and control. Its spires stabbed the clouds. Its walls, ribbed with iron and shadow, looked less like fortifications and more like a place that swallowed things and didn’t spit them back.

Inside the carriage, two figures sat opposite one another.

Cyrene, radiant in lilac and white, looked carved from calm itself. Her posture was gentle, unmoving, her eyes fixed on the window though they no longer seemed to see. She wore no crown, no jewels, just the soft shimmer of dignity, like a lantern refusing to dim even when the wind howled around it.

Across from her, Phainon vibrated with restrained fury. His fists dug into his knees, his boots scuffed from pacing earlier that morning. He looked out of place in this velvet-lined carriage, all broad shoulders and muscles, every inch of him a mismatched piece in the doomed puzzle.

He had faced wild beasts. Survived storms at sea. Once fought off a pack of dire hounds with nothing but a splintered torch and a branch.

And none of it felt as terrible as this journey.

"You don’t have to do this," he said, with a voice that was rough and low like gravel underfoot.

Cyrene blinked slowly, turning her gaze to meet his. She smiled, a small, aching curve of the mouth that stung worse than any blade. "Yes, I do."

“No.” Phainon leaned forward, his gaze hardened into a glare. “No, you don’t. This isn’t duty, Cyrene. It’s suicide.”

Her brows lifted slightly, patient, but wary.

“We have heard everything about this brute,” Phainon continued. “This so-called king. This prince of lions. They say he kills anyone who disobeys him. Killed his own father. Burned half his city to prove a point. You think offering him a flower from the fields is going to stop him?”

“They say he’s cruel,” she murmured. “But also strategic.”

“Strategic?” Phainon scoffed. “Is that what we’re calling bloodlust now?”

She said nothing. Her silence was maddening.

He slammed a fist lightly against the wooden wall of the carriage. “You’re not a shield, Cyrene. You’re not some bartering chip.”

“If I don’t go,” she said, still gentle, “we'll be in trouble.”

Phainon looked at her, jaw clenched. “Then let's run.”

Her brows rose in surprise.

“We’ll turn the carriage around right now,” he said. “Go to the mountains. Disappear.”

“And then Kremnos sends armies,” she replied. “You’ve seen what they do. I won’t bring that our home. Our families, the children. They will be in danger.”

“There has to be another way.”

“There isn’t.”

“There is.” His voice cracked. “Let me the one who face them.”

Cyrene’s breath caught. “They are waiting for the crown princess, not our mightiest swordsman, Phainon."

"Then I'll just go as you,” he said, surging forward, his hands open, desperate. “Let me take your place. I’ll wear the veil, hide under lace and smiles, and walk into that mad lion’s den for you. You’re not the only one who can lie through a smile.”

“Phainon…”

“I can do that, Cyrene,” he pressed on, undeterred. “If he wants someone to glare at, let him glare at me. If he wants blood for broken promises, then he can try to take mine.”

Cyrene laughed, but it wasn’t real. It was brittle, just a sound which people make when they’re holding something sharp inside.

“You? Posing as me?” she said, managing a hint of amusement. "Phainon, you’d crush the carriage just by stepping in. Do you even know how to curtsey?”

“I’ll invent a new one,” Phainon said, deadpan. “The warbow curtsey. Involves knocking out his guards with a smile.”

“You’re too tall.”

“I’ll kneel.”

“You’re too loud.”

“I’ll whisper.”

“You can’t even sit still.”

“I’m sitting now, aren’t I?”

She bit back another laugh, this time laced with affection. “Phainon…”

“I’m serious.” He reached across the space between them, grasping her hands in his. “Let me do this. Let me be the one who walks through those gates.”

Her hands were small in his, soft and warm, and trembling faintly. But she didn’t pull away.

“I can’t let you go there,” he said. “To him. Not when I could go in your place.”

She looked away, to the narrowing horizon. The mountains now loomed, jagged as shattered glass. The air smelled colder.

“I can’t ask that of you,” she whispered.

“You’re not asking,” he replied. “I’m forcing you.”

Silence settled, heavier than before.

Phainon leaned closer, his voice was softened. “You had dreams. That orchard by the river. A library for children. Don’t let them rot in some tower while that bastard sharpens his crown with your bones.”

She closed her eyes.

“And what about your dream?” she asked, barely audible.

He hesitated. Then said, “This is my dream. To keep you safe. To not sit here and watch you be sent off like livestock.”

Cyrene’s hands curled tighter in his.

The carriage jolted slightly. The road now wound into rock. Distant horns began to rise, a low, dreadful note that told them Kremnos was near.

Cyrene sighed, hesitated before asking, softly, “What about your promise?”

“Promise?”

“You told me once,” she said, “that there was someone you were waiting for.”

His lips parted, seemingly wanted to say something but the words were stuck.

“I remember,” she continued. “You said there was a boy you met when you were young, when you always said too busy to read with me. A boy that was so pretty, wild thing, always hiding in the trees. You gave him fish and stories. He never told you his name. But you said... if fate was kind, you’d meet again.”

A long pause followed.

Then, Phainon smiled. Not the usual grin that came with mischief or teasing, but something gentler. Something quieter.

“I’m still waiting,” he said.

Her gaze softened. “Even now?”

“Especially now.”

He leaned back against the carriage wall, his hands finally relaxing in his lap.

“I don’t know where he went. Maybe he grew up and forgot. Maybe he’s across the sea. Maybe he never really existed at all.” He looked toward the horizon. “But I never stopped waiting. Just in case.”

Cyrene watched him in silence, heart aching in places she hadn’t expected.

Then Phainon turned to her, his grin returning, brighter now, with that stubborn light he always carried like armor. “So, you’ll have to meet him on my stead.”

"Me...?"

He nodded. “If you ever see him, some peculiar but beautiful boy with gold eyes and happened to know someone named Phainon, tell him I waited. Tell him I became something worth waiting for. A hero, maybe. Or just a loud idiot who couldn’t sit still.”

His grin faltered just a little. “Tell him I didn’t forget. Maybe make him regret not finding me faster.”

The weight of that request settled into the quiet, like a thread tying them together even as the world split paths beneath them.

Cyrene reached out and took his hand again.

“If I let you go…”

“Then you live,” he said. “You live, and you plant those trees. You laugh under the sun. You build that library. If I'm lucky, you find that boy and tell him my story.”

"And if I said no...?"

"If he accepted you then so be it. If not, I will make trouble enough for us so I'll be the only one to go. I'll stay with you eitherway." 

She searched his face. There was no boyish mischief now. No sarcastic grin. Just Phainon, bare, fierce, and so painfully real it broke something in her.

Her lips trembled. “They’ll kill you if they find out.”

“Only if I lose.”

“And if you do lose?”

“Then at least I die fighting for something that mattered.”

"Phainon..."

"Hey, I think of you as my own sister. I don't want anything bad happened to you. Please, Cyrene. Follow my whim this one last time, okay?"

Another grin, another facade and yet, Cyrene couldn't bring herself to hate it. She exhaled shakily, her whole frame trembling. Then, slowly, achingly, she nodded.

“Alright,” she whispered. “Alright. You win. I doubt it will end peacefully eitherway...”

Relief hit him so hard his breath caught. He pulled her into a tight hug, burying his face in her shoulder. She hugged back, fiercely, like she didn’t know if she’d ever get another chance.

“You’ll need a dress,” she murmured against him.

“And rouge,” he added. “Apparently warlords like flushed cheeks.”

She laughed again, this time breathlessly, shaky with emotion.

When they pulled apart, there were tears on her lashes.

“I’ll make sure you get there safely,” she said. “And then I’ll vanish. They won’t trace me.”

“You’re the best,” Phainon murmured.

“I’m the foolish one who said yes.”

The carriage rolled on, and Kremnos rose before them, vast, merciless, and waiting.

But now, Phainon would be the one to face it.

**

chapters.title: Ten Days, Ten Nights.
chapters.html:
The gates of Kremnos groaned open, iron grinding against iron, like the jaws of some ancient beast preparing to swallow the world.


Beyond them, the capital stretched out in cruel elegance.


The plaza was pulsed with life.


Soldiers stood in rigid ranks, their armor dark and glinting like obsidian glass. Civilians crowded every staircase, balcony, and rooftop. Craning necks, fanning themselves with cloth, eager to catch a glimpse of the bride offered in exchange for peace.


The flower of Aedes Elysiae.


The girl who, rumor whispered, could coax dragon to sleep, turn storms soft, and charm tyrants with a single look.


The carriage slowed to a halt beneath the looming stone archway, flanked by towering spears and flaming braziers. The silence was loud, waiting, thick with breath held in suspense.


A herald stepped forward, his hands trembling against the scroll he unrolled. His voice, thin but determined, rang out.


“By order of pact and preservation, we present Her Highness, Princess Cyrene of Aedes Elysiae!”


The crowd hushed.


The carriage door creaked.


And out stepped nearly two meters of veiled muscle, wrapped in a pale blue, sleeveless, delicately embroidered, fit like it had given up trying. The bodice clung to his broad chest with the desperation. The hem flapped wildly around his shins. His arms, thick with muscle, were completely exposed. His shoulders alone looked capable of carrying multiple sacks of flours with ease.


Behind the carriage, one of the Elysian escorts leaned toward another, his voice barely above a horrified whisper. “There’s no way they’ll fall for this.”


A ripple passed through the crowd, not laughter. Not scorn.


But confusion. Then awe.


Then came the murmurs.


And not the ones Phainon had braced for.


“By the name of Nikador, she’s massive.”


“Oh my strife, look at those arms. She could cradle a grown man like a baby.”


“Or crush one. I'd volunteer.”


“That’s not a princess, that’s a divine punishment sent to smite the unworthy.”


“Look at that jawline. She could chew iron.”


“Elysiae’s breeding warriors now, not wives. Kremnos will be pleased.”


Phainon’s eyes widened behind the veil.


( Wait. What? )


He’d expected mockery. Disgust. Maybe even a spear aimed between the eyes.


But they weren’t laughing.


They were… impressed?


A child clung to their mother’s shawl, tugging insistently. “Mama, is that really the princess?”


The mother, eyes fixed in reverent awe, whispered back, “Of course. Look at her biceps. That’s royalty.”


"She looks so strong!"


Phainon froze, mid-step, nearly tripping on the hem of his dress. His brain short-circuited.


( They thought this... THIS was attractive?)


He had spent the entire journey preparing himself for arrows, guillotines, and political outrage.


Not compliments.


Behind the veil, his expression went from alarmed to absolutely feral with secondhand embarrassment.


But the commentary was just warming up.


“Those thighs,” someone whispered. “I bet she can break a neck with those.”


“If she does become queen, I volunteer as her concubine. I’ll cook. I’ll clean. I’ll raise her children.”


“She can make the children herself, I’ll just stand there.”


“Do you think she lifts stone slabs for fun? Because I’m willing to be the slab.”


The escort behind him let out a choked wheeze that was either a laugh or a prayer for deliverance. Phainon shot him a death glare.


More voices shouted over each other:


“Look at how the dress is struggling. It’s an honor to be crushed like that.”


“Now I see all those rumours are true. Not only vicious dragon, even I would sleep at her presence.”


“She’s battle-ready! Like she could duel her own husband on the wedding night!”


“Bless the titans for giving her calves like that. May the royal bedframe survive.”


Phainon was halfway to combusting on the spot.


( This isn’t going to plan, he screamed internally. They were supposed to laugh. Or riot. Or arrest me! )


But instead, they were swooning.


His spine stiffened. His arms instinctively flexed at his sides as he straightened, trying not to hear the extremely detailed description whisper but it was no use, the words were too loud as he made his way through the crowd.


He heard someone say, “If she doesn’t marry the king, I’ll build her a throne myself.”


“Forget marrying her. I just want to see her sword collection. And maybe her biceps. And maybe her thighs, up close, respectfully but urgently.”


“She’s got a fine body like a siege weapon. I'm in love.”


Phainon exhaled shakily through his nose.


The only thing keeping him walking now was sheer stubbornness and the knowledge that if he tripped, the story would haunt him across the continent.


And so, under a storm of wildly inappropriate thirst, praise, and declarations of devotion, Phainon walked.


The gown tugged at his thighs with every step. His back was straight. His face a carefully composed portrait of shy nobility (while internally screaming). By the time he reached the steps of the palace, he was seriously considering spontaneous combustion as a viable escape route.


However, somewhere between disbelief and dying, he thought that Kremnos, it seemed, had no appetite for delicate glass dolls in frilly gowns. They wanted sharp edges. Power wrapped in beauty. And apparently, they thought Phainon looked like a divine threat in a dress.


His spine straightened instinctively, his steps still awkward, but steadier now. Maybe this wasn’t going to be as bad as he thought. Maybe, if he played it right, he could bluff his way through the ceremony, buy some time, escape under cover of night. He told himself that everything would be okay.


But then, when the doors of the great hall opened, every emotion that lingered in his chest scattered like ash.


The Castrum Kremnos was not made to welcome. It was built to intimidate. Towering black columns lined the corridor like spears held by titans. The red banners above were stitched with the sigils of conquest, heavy with history, stained at their fringes by time and fire. The light came not from chandeliers, but from braziers burning cold and blue, like the memory of flame. But even all that grandeur paled compared to the figure on the throne.


At the far end of the hall, seated like a god bored of prayers, was Mydeimos.


He didn’t sit with the decorum expected of royalty. His back rested heavily against the throne, legs spread wide in a way that claimed the space without apology. One arm draped over the armrest, the other loosely holding a gem-cut goblet of something pinkish.


His clothing was half-armor, half-regalia. Red and black with golden accents, his cloak sweeping from one shoulder, leaving his torso exposed, scarless, yet streaked with red markings that almost looked painted on by fire. Ornamental plates guarded his forearms and legs, designed more for intimidation than defense. A massive sun emblem clasped his belt, gleaming like a warning.


And his face... Eyes like molten gold. Hair tousled, yet regal, the strands shifting between blonde and flame depending on how the light caught. His features were sharp, but not cruel. Beautiful, in a way that felt wrong to look at too long.


But even behind his veil, Phainon stared.


He had imagined a monster. A brute of a man with madness in his eyes and blood on his hands. But this was something else entirely.


A living weapon wrapped in gold and flame.

And just a little, just a little, he was reminded by a certain person he missed dearly each day.

( Could it be... No, it can't be... )

“You’re supposed to bow,” came Kremnos' chancellor, Krateros, low reminder from his side.

Phainon jolted.

He quickly dipped into the most awkward curtsy ever performed by a man his size in a dress a dozen centimetres too short.

When he straightened, his voice didn’t sound like his own.

“Your Majesty,” he said, trying not to flinch beneath that intense gaze. “I am Princess Cyrene of Aedes Elysiae.”

A lie.

One veiled, trembling lie, delivered to a man known for smelling fear like a hound.

And Mydeimos had yet to say a single word.

He just stared.

Unmoving. Unblinking. Golden eyes sharp as blades, narrowed ever so slightly behind the rim of his goblet.

Phainon shifted under the veil. A bead of sweat rolled down his back. Surely, everyone in the room could hear how loud his heart was hammering.

The silence stretched like drawn wire.

Finally, one of the Aedes delegates stepped forward, clearing his throat.

“We present our Crown Princess,” he said, formally, “to humbly atone for our failure to fulfill the promised tribute. A gesture of good faith. Of peace. In hopes that His Majesty might offer mercy upon Aedes Elysiae.”

Still no response.

Mydeimos took another sip from his drink.

And somehow, that made it worse.

Phainon should have been focusing on the diplomacy. The lives at stake. The fact that the so-called bride was him, in a veil, lying through his teeth to a king who could likely crush a man with one hand.

But all of that slipped to the background just because Mydeimos lifted his goblet again.

The light caught his movement like a spotlight, focusing on how his muscles shifting. His lips parted just enough for the rim to settle, and he drank slow. Deliberate. Like nothing in this hall mattered more than whatever filled that glass.

The curve of his throat moved as he swallowed, a low motion that was too elegant for someone with a reputation for violence.

Phainon didn’t mean to keep watching. He really didn’t.

But as he drank, a single drop escaped the rim.

It slid down the corner of his mouth, clinging.

And then Mydei’s tongue darted out, quick and effortless, to swipe over it.

That simple motion nearly short-circuited Phainon’s brain.

It wasn’t seductive, not deliberately. There was no pretense, no showmanship. It was just efficient. Clean. But something about how casual it was felt far more dangerous than any sword in the room.

Phainon’s eyes tracked the motion, his breath catching.

A drop of juice. A flick of a tongue. And suddenly he wasn’t sure if he was here to save his country or if he wanted to watch Mydeimos lick something again.

And that was the problem.

He wasn’t supposed to be beautiful.

He was supposed to be a tyrant. A brute. An animal on a throne.

But instead, he sat there draped in crimson and power, drinking like he wanted everyone in the room to see how sexy he was.

Phainon could feel his face heating beneath the veil, his eyes kept drifting back to Mydeimos’s mouth.

And his heart wouldn’t slow down.

When the delegate jabbed him sharply in the ribs, Phainon jumped like he’d been caught stealing.

Phainon blinked, startled. “O-oh. Yes.”

He snapped into a quick kneel. “Your Majesty, I beg for your mercy on behalf of my people.”

Mydeimos finally stirred.

He lowered the goblet.

“I’m not marrying anyone,” he said flatly. “Send her back.”

The room tensed.

Several of the nobles exchanged stunned glances. One even mouthed, “But she’s perfect.”

“I have no use for silk and songs,” Mydeimos continued, sternly. “Crops. Maybe minerals. That’s what I prefer. Not politics in perfume.”

Phainon’s lips parted. “But...!”

“No.”

It was a dismissal. A final one.

Phainon’s mind raced. This was supposed to work. If he was sent back, it would all fall apart. The threat, the insult, the risk to Cyrene and their country... Phainon shook his head. He hadn’t worn this godsdamned dress, crossed kingdoms, and risked public humiliation just to be dismissed like a dull coin.

In a moment of pure desperation, words slipped out of his mouth before his brain could stop them.

“Then fight me for it.”

The silence after Phainon’s challenge didn’t just stretch, it suffocated. It swirled around the marble pillars and wrapped its fingers around every breath in the hall.

Even the torchlight flickered, as if startled.

For one terrifying moment, Phainon thought no one had heard him. That perhaps, if he stood very still, the titans might allow the words to vanish like mist.

However for the first time, Mydeimos moved more than an inch. He leaned forward, and a slow, amused smirk tugged at the corner of his lips.

And somehow, he looked even more stunning.

Phainon’s pulse slammed against his throat. Every instinct screamed to kneel, apologize, laugh it off, pretend it was a joke. But he wouldn't hear it any longer. Not when those molten eyes met his.

“Fight you?” Mydeimos repeated like he was questioning Phainon's sanity.

Phainon’s mouth went dry. He nodded anyway.

Mydeimos stood abruptly, his crimson drapery swaying like a fallen banner. The Young King took a single step forward, and the crowd held its breath.

His eyes were locked against Phainon's despite the veil. Sharp, unwavering and Phainon answered with a scowl, trying to assert his own dominance in the enemy's territory.

“Very well,” he said simply. That single word cracked through the tension like steel against stone.

"Hephaestion." He called out without even looking behind. 

Hephaestion, looming and quiet, bowed his head slightly at the summon. No one else dared move.

“Take our guest to the colosseum,” Mydeimos instructed. “Let her choose her weapon.”

Somehow, there was something almost indulgent in his voice, but maybe it was nothing but a fleeting amusement.

"Over here, Princess." Phainon gave a last glance to the delegates from Aedes Elysiae and raised his thumbs up, as if telling them not to worry before he followed the long-haired Kremoan.

The path from the throne hall to the colosseum curved along a ridge of dark stone, overlooking Kremnos’s jagged rooftops and narrow alleys like a spine of shadow. The mountain wind bit at Phainon’s exposed calves, his borrowed dress fluttering around him like a bedsheet trying to escape.

Hephaestion walked beside him in silence at first, tall, solemn, with long golden hair tied in a ribbon and eyes as sharp as a drawn blade. Then, as they descended into the shadow of the colosseum, he finally spoke.

"You’re brave," Hephaestion said. "Or foolish."

Phainon glanced over, brushing his veil back from his face. "It’s usually both."

They passed through the outer arch, where carved lions flanked the gate, jaws open mid-roar. Inside, the walls curved like the ribcage of a beast. The air smelled of old blood and sweat, sand and iron.

"No one’s ever bested our king," Hephaestion continued, almost gently. "Not in a duel. Not even close. No one even ever made it in piece."

"Then I’ll be the first to walk out alive," Phainon said, chin lifting with stubborn fire.

Hephaestion glanced at him, as if measuring those words against reality, then nodded once. "Good luck, Princess."

Phainon didn’t correct him.

He didn’t change out of the gown either. He couldn’t, not yet. Even if he failed here, the story of Cyrene had to stay intact.

He moved to the weapon rack. Most of the choices gleamed with Kremnoan design, curved axes, hooked spears, vicious flails designed to maim rather than kill. But Phainon reached for a sword. A simple one. Balanced and heavy. Something familiar.

He gripped the hilt, gave it a test swing, and exhaled.

( Let's do this. )

Phainon put his veil away, letting his short hair freed and heaving a long sigh before he walked down the tunnel. By the end of it, the arena gates creaked open.

Stone steps led down to the sunlit circle, surrounded by rows upon rows of benches. Already, the seats were filling, guards, generals, courtiers, and even civilians who had followed the rumor of a foreign bride challenging their war-king.

And at the center of the colosseum, standing in a patch of shadowed light, was Mydeimos.

Phainon stepped down, the sword in his hand, the wind tugging at his hair. He could feel eyes on him again, some skeptical, others hungry for spectacle.

Mydeimos was already waiting.

He wore those same scarlet-gold gauntlets on his hands and forearms, shimmering with etched runes. His cloak had been discarded. His torso glowed in the sun, every line of muscle like something artistic, chiselled by an artist than battle. Those red markings looked even brighter now, trailing like embers along his chest and ribs, further slithering to his back.

Phainon stopped a few paces away, eyebrows raised.

“No weapon?” he asked, tightening his grip on the sword.

Mydeimos rolled one shoulder, the metal of his gauntlet catching the light like it wanted to blind someone. “I figured my knuckles would suffice,” he said. “Against a princess.”

Something about the way he said princess made Phainon bristle.

“Oh, we’ll see about that.”

He didn’t wait for ceremony.

He lunged first.

Steel arced through the air. Mydeimos didn’t dodge, he blocked it with a single upraised forearm. The clang rang out like a hammer on an anvil. Sparks flew. Phainon staggered back.

That gauntlet had dented his blade.

Phainon grinned. “All right. You’re not just pretty.”

Mydeimos tilted his head slightly. “You talk too much.”

He struck.

Phainon barely twisted aside in time. The fist missed his ribs by inches, wind howling past his ear. He jumped back again, panting, circling.

The next exchange came faster. Sword met metal again and again, sparks trailing each hit like fireworks. Phainon moved quick, using reach, angles, speed. Mydeimos, in contrast, was all force, every punch like a battering ram, his body a wall of relentless momentum.

By the fifth minute, Phainon’s skirt was already tangled around his knees.

“Damn this thing,” he hissed, eyes darting for an opening.

He dropped into a low crouch and with one sharp tug, ripped the side of the gown up to his thigh, fabric tearing in a long, satisfying sound. The wind rushed against his bare leg, and finally, movement.

The audience gasped. A few cheered.

“Oh Nikador,” someone whispered. “She’s magnificent.”

"Did you see that thigh?!"

“She’s going to kill him with beauty.”

The pace shifted.

Phainon spun low, sword slashing in a half-arc meant to test the edge of Mydeimos’s guard. But the king pivoted smoothly and met it with the back of his wrist, deflecting the blow with ease. Then he countered, fast.

Phainon blocked just in time, the impact vibrating all the way to his elbow. He staggered. Mydeimos followed.

Another blow.

Then another.

The third one slammed into his side, knocking him across the sand. Phainon rolled with it, coughing.

( Damn. He hit hard. )

Still, he got up.

Sword raised again, body aching, dress flapping like a flag in the wind.

“You really are stubborn. Don't you know when to stop?” Mydeimos said, walking toward him.

“Says the man fighting a girl in heels,” Phainon shot back.

That finally drew a flicker of amusement from the king’s eyes.

Then, they clashed again.

Steel against gauntlet.

Ripped dress fluttering.

Blood blooming from a shallow cut on Phainon’s lip.

At first, it was a spectacle. A bride in torn silk wielding a soldier’s blade against the indomitable king of Kremnos. The stands roared with laughter, with disbelief, with bets placed and drinks spilled. The courtiers smirked. The nobles leaned forward, expecting it to end in minutes.

And then the minutes turned to hours.

And they were still fighting.

The clash of steel against golden gauntlet echoed like thunder inside the marble colosseum. Phainon moved like a storm barely contained by skin, sharp, relentless, all instinct and stubborn grit. His sword carved arcs through the air, crashing against Mydeimos’s arms, striking speck of fire with every blow.

But Mydeimos didn’t flinch.

The Kremnoan king moved with terrifying precision. No wasted motion. Every step forward forced Phainon back. Every block came with the promise of a counter. He didn’t dodge, he endured. And each time Phainon’s blade kissed his skin, he hissed but he kept moving like it didn't bother him.

As if the man were carved from something beyond flesh.

Phainon knew exhaustion intimately. He’d sparred with giants, swum across rivers with weights strapped to his legs, held plank positions until his body shook. But this wasn’t training. This was survival. And Mydeimos fought like he hadn’t bled in years.

And through it all, Phainon’s mind buzzed with adrenaline, pure excitement. Along the way, he swung his sword not only for winning, but for the enjoyment of the battle itself.

By the third day, Phainon stabbed Mydeimos so deep that blood spluttered on the dirt. A normal human would be dying. Yet, the insane king laughed it off, and managed to send Phainon flew with a single punch and easily ripped his own sleeve to serve as tourniquet.

By the fourth, Phainon’s sword cracked near the hilt.

By the fifth, it shattered.

He barely registered the gasp from the crowd as steel exploded from his grip in a spray of shrapnel. He stood there, panting, holding the jagged remains, heart pounding against his ribs like a war drum.

And Mydeimos, always so unreadable, lifted his arms.

Then tossed aside both gauntlets.

They landed with a weighty clang, rolling against the edge of the arena.

The crowd fell into stunned silence.

Then Mydeimos raised one bare hand and beckoned.

Phainon charged.

No swords. No armor. No formality.

They fought with fists and fury.

Mydeimos' punches were calculated, brutally effective, aimed for joints, pressure points, the ribs. Phainon countered with sheer tenacity. Grapples, elbows, knees. He took hits that would have felled other men and kept getting up, eyes blazing beneath sweat-soaked lashes.

They fought until their hands were bloodied.

Until the dirt clung to their skin like a second flesh.

Every blow carried the weight of a kingdom behind it. And somehow, Phainon matched him. He bled from the mouth. From his scalp. His arms screamed with strain. But he didn’t stop.

Neither did Mydeimos.

They moved like mirrored beasts across the sand-strewn marble, gritting their teeth, sweat rolling down their spines, blood mixing into the dust.

And the crowd, once rowdy, became silence.

Because days passed.

Actual days.

No one understood how it was possible. How these two bodies, both young, both battered but still forced themselves to keep going.

People came and went. Spectators were replaced by fresh ones. Nobles left and returned, eyes wide in disbelief. Merchants sold refreshments at the edge of the colosseum. A bard wrote a song on the third day and began performing it during the fifth night.

Even dignitaries from rival nations came to watch.

They weren’t sure what they were witnessing.

A duel?

A declaration?

Or something ancient, something primal, that had outgrown its purpose.

By the seventh day, even the moon watched them.

High in the sky, casting silver over the battered floor where two men circled one another, neither backing down.

Phainon no longer thought of Cyrene. Or diplomacy. Or Aedes Elysiae.

He thought of breathing. Of Mydeimos’s eyes, how bright they were, how unyielding. How he wanted to make the arrogance shatter.

And Mydeimos, though silent, seemed just as caught. Every time Phainon rose again from the dust, something sparked behind those golden irises. Not fury. Not annoyance.

Recognition.

By the tenth day, neither could speak.

Phainon had lost count of how many times he’d been thrown into the ground. He was more bruise than skin now. His legs trembled with each step, but still carried him forward.

Mydeimos’s strikes had slowed. Not from mercy, but exhaustion. Even his immortal body had its limits. His chest rose and fell with ragged breaths. His arms, normally steady as statues, now faltered between attacks.

Then, finally, Phainon stumbled.

His leg gave out. He crashed onto his hands and knees, breathing like he was drowning in dry air.

He didn’t rise.

Not immediately.

He could hear the throb of his pulse behind his eyes, the pounding of a thousand heartbeats stacked in a row. Blood ran down his jaw. His vision blurred.

And across from him, Mydeimos stood still for a long moment, then staggered back one step.

Then another.

Then knelt.

The audience didn’t cheer.

They didn’t dare.

Because something sacred had just occurred. Something that could not be celebrated with noise.

Two warriors had stripped themselves down to their very souls.

And for the first time in ten nights, they stopped.

Phainon lifted his head.

Mydeimos looked at him.

Their gazes locked across the blood-stained arena, across days of pain and sweat and breathless rage.

Ten days. Ten nights.

Neither had won.

And neither had truly lost.

Phainon laughed, or tried to. It came out as a breathless, choked wheeze.

“You’re not even human,” he muttered in a husky whisper.

Across from him, Mydeimos exhaled slow.

“Neither are you,” he said.

The dust still hung in the air when Mydeimos rose.

Blood streaked his bare arms, drying into rust. His chest heaved, but his voice, when he parted his own lips again, was clear as polished steel.

“Aedes Elysiae,” he said, loud enough for the entire colosseum to hear, “shall be spared for the next ten years.”

A stunned silence followed.

Then came a rumble, gasps, whispers, even cheers. The tension that had gripped the arena for days finally cracked, spilling into disbelief. A whole decade without tax, without fear of Kremnoan hunger at their gates. It was more than mercy.

It was a miracle.

Phainon, still half-kneeling in the dirt, lifted his head.

A weak, crooked smile pulled at his lips. “That’s... good,” he panted. “Thank you.”

His body screamed for rest. His knees barely held him. But his grin widened all the same. He hadn’t won. Not in the usual sense. But he had gotten what he came for. The fields of Elysiae would be safe. Cyrene could plant her orchard. The children would get their library. He had done it.

“But.”

The word fell like a stone.

The crowd thrown into silence again. Even the air went still.

Mydeimos turned, gaze cutting sharp beneath the falling light.

“I’ll pardon the tribute,” he said. “But I will not ignore deception.”

Phainon's eyelashes fluttered fast, heart stumbling.

The king took a slow step forward, his gaze was once again as cold as stone.

“Did you really think I wouldn’t notice? You must've treat me like an idiot.”

Phainon didn’t answer.

Mydeimos’s voice dropped low, quieter.

“You’re lucky I let it play out this long,” Mydeimos said, stepping back. “You’re even luckier I found it... entertaining.”

Then, louder, “Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon’s grin faltered.

Gasps broke through the arena like sparks.

Mydei’s stare didn’t waver.

“You are to be detained,” he said coldly like delivering a verdict, “until I decide what to do with you.”

The crowd rippled with disbelief as murmurs caught fire across the seats: 

"Phainon? Not Cyrene?"

"The fight hadn’t been a bride’s offering at all. It had been a bluff."

"They are trying to fool us!"

Hephaestion moved first, giving a brief nod before signaling the guards.

Phainon let out a short laugh, half breath, half wheeze. “Guess the dress really didn’t sell it, huh?”

Two armored soldiers approached. Phainon didn’t flinch, didn’t move. His hands fell to his thighs in surrender. He was covered in grime and sweat, fabric clinging to him like wet silk, but his eyes still gleamed with mischief.

“Even so,” he said, flashing a tired grin up at the king, “thank you. For sparing my home.”

Mydeimos’s eyes flicked toward him. Then, barely audible over the rustling crowd, Mydeimos murmured, “You’re a fool.” He turned and strode from the colosseum.

Phainon watched him go, lips still curled at the edges. He didn’t fight the guards. He didn’t run. He let them take him, stumbling slightly as he was led out of the blood-soaked ring.

**
