The door had closed behind the guards with a soft click, but instead of the chill of iron bars or the stink of a dungeon, Phainon was met with polished marble, faintly glowing lanterns, and a bed big enough to drown in.


He stared in silence, dirt still clinging to his skin, his dress in tatters and half-stuck to the dried blood at his ribs.


"...Huh."


It only got stranger.


Attendants came, quiet, efficient, avoiding his eyes but showing no sign of hostility. They led him to a private bath: warm, fragrant with something floral and spiced, the steam curling like welcome arms. One helped peel away the ruined gown while another laid out fresh cloths and bandages. He didn’t speak much, just watched them with mild suspicion, flinching when gentle hands dabbed at the wounds along his side and shoulders.


Then came the food.


By the time Phainon was dressed again, loose cotton shirt, soft pants, skin clean and bruises tended, he returned to find a small table laid with roasted meats, honey-glazed roots, seasoned greens, and a pitcher of chilled grape juice. Everything smelled sinfully good.


"...This isn’t a prison," he muttered, picking up a fork. "This is... even better than a room service provided by an inn."


He ate. Slowly at first, then with the hunger of someone who hadn’t seen proper food in ten days. The fatigue in his limbs dragged heavier with every bite. And yet, some voice at the back of his head whispered that maybe this was a trick. A final comfort before a blade. The calm before execution. Or maybe this was their version of a last supper.


By the time night had deepened, Phainon found himself alone again. He drifted out to the balcony of his high room, the cool air brushing past his still-damp hair. Below, Kremnos flickered in red and gold, torchlight, watchfires, the eerie stillness of a city that never truly slept.


He leaned his elbows against the carved stone railing and sighed.


“No regrets,” he told the wind.


It was true.


He had no regrets.


Not for Cyrene, who could now chased her dream. Not for the people of Aedes Elysiae, who wouldn’t go hungry next decade. He would do it again if given the choice.


But...


He closed his eyes. Rested his cheek against one hand.


“I never got to see him again,” he said softly.


The boy.


That strange, feral thing he’d met under a tree so many years ago.


A child who barely spoke, who rubbed his face when he almost cried, who said he liked pomegranate juice with milk. A kid who all sharp glances and sudden silences, always hiding like the world might bite him. A kitten-brained little thing who always looked so startled whenever Phainon got too close, like he wasn’t sure if he wanted to run or stay. 


And yet, Phainon had adored him. Helplessly. Unchangingly.


He chuckled a little, remembering how the boy had flailed and blushed after that tiny kiss. How he’d bolted off like a scaredy-cat, but not before kissing Phainon’s cheek and making a promise after all.


“I’ll be back,” he’d said.


And Phainon, young and lovestruck, had believed it with all his heart.


His fingers curled over the balcony edge.


“…Wonder what he looks like now,” he murmured, a smile tugging faintly at the corners of his lips. “Taller by then, obviously. Graceful. Maybe he wears robes. Or glasses. Maybe he reads poetry by the riverbank and still talks like he’s trying to sound braver than he is.”


His heart warmed at the image.


That kid would have grown into someone… beautiful. Gentle, maybe. The kind of man who offered smiles like secrets, who knew how to soothe storms with a glance. Someone who baked bread and recited old songs and maybe, just maybe, still looked at Phainon like he was a little bit dazzling.


He closed his eyes.


His smile softened.


“Or maybe…”


Maybe he wasn’t delicate at all.


Maybe he was—


His thoughts shifted unwillingly, traitorously, to the throne. To the body that sat there like it owned the entire world. Mydeimos, with his red-marked chest which eerily similar to the young boy, muscles dusted in gold light, that smirk like he knew too well how to sin.

Phainon opened his eyes and blinked hard.


“No. Absolutely not,” he muttered. “That’s not the same person. Just because he has the same eyes doesn’t mean—”


His heart thumped once. Hard.


“The hair. Sure. And maybe the markings too. And okay, fine, the eyes are almost the same shade of gold, but—”


His voice dropped into a whisper. “There’s no way that sweet, skittish boy turned into that, brute. That's not a cute kitty, that's a vicious, rabid lion.”


He scowled at the moon.


“No way. My kitty cat won't be such arrogant, half-naked warlord with smirks carved out of sin and a drinking habit that looks like it belongs in a tavern play. That’s not him. That can’t be him.”


His hands clenched the balcony edge.


“He had… innocence, my kitten. He flinched when I touched his shoulder, blushed adorably when I kissed him and ran away like his tail was on fire after peck my cheek.”


But his brain refused to stop. No matter how much he glared into the stars.


Mydeimos standing in the great hall, hips cocked in that infuriating way, lips brushing the rim of his goblet like he knew exactly what it was doing to anyone watching. The way his tongue had darted out...

Phainon swallowed.


( What if I got to do that? )


( Just once. )


Just once, let his fingers trail that jawline, trace the heat of skin marked by battle, tilt that smug face toward him and kiss the taste of his drink right off his mouth.


( No,! NO! stop that— )


Phainon sucked in a breath. But his mind kept spiralling.


It dragged him back to that moment, to their fight.


Mydeimos, with blood down his cheek and a wild gleam in his eyes, like the fight had brought him to life. He had smiled, grinned. Wide. Reckless.


And Phainon, in the middle of a brawl that might’ve cost his life, had looked at that grin and thought miserably to himself:


(...Damn. he looked unfairly good. Blood shouldn’t look that good on anyone. )


He remembered thinking that it was the first time someone had looked at him like that in a fight. Like he was someone worthy.


Even now, he could recall how Mydeimos’ hair had stuck to his temples, damp with sweat and streaked with blood. He didn’t wince on pain. Or maybe he just didn’t mind bleeding. His skin was marked, smeared with dirt and scarlet streaks, shining faintly where muscle flexed under every blow. There was a madness in him then, but it wasn’t the frothing-at-the-mouth kind.


It was breathtaking. Ethereal.


“No,” Phainon muttered. “No, you do not get to think about his eyes right now.”


Then came the worst part.


A growing pressure. Low. Warm.


He blinked. Looked down. And slapped both hands over his groin in horror.


“Are you kidding me?”


He hissed through his teeth, backing away from the railing like it was cursed.  His voice pitched higher. “You think that violent brute was hot?!”


Phainon shifted. His thighs pressed together.


His expression dropped further into abject horror.


“Are you serious right now?” he hissed, gripping the edge of his tunic like he could yank the thoughts out of his bloodstream. “He threatened to kill me! He almost did kill me! And you’re getting ideas because he happened to have… sexy body and glowing eyes and a face that made my knees weak?!”


Somewhere deep in his chest, and elsewhere, his body disagreed. Just kept throbbing from memories and the ache of his own damned imagination.


It remembered the weight of Mydeimos on top of him, both of them panting, slick with sweat and dirt and fury. It remembered his hands, rough, calloused, wrapped around Phainon’s wrist, the pressure of his thigh pinning him down, the low rasp of his voice inches from his ear, coaxing him to give up. That look in his eyes, sharp, golden, focused. Like a predator. Like a man who took whatever he wanted and made the prey crave for it.


And the image had taken root. It bloomed fast, shameful and vivid.


His brain concocted a new scene. Mydeimos pinning him to the mattress the same way he did in the colosseum, bodies slick, muscles straining. Not with swords this time, but with breath, with pressure, with heat. Grappling not to win, but to see who could make the other fall apart first. The kind of wrestling where no one pulled away first. Where mouths clashed instead of blades.


He imagined the sound Mydeimos might make, low, ragged, not cruel but hungry. Like he hadn’t been fed in years and Phainon was a feast of sweat and adrenaline and skin. Mydeimos would bite down on Phainon’s shoulder just to hear the sound he'd make. Phainon flipping him over with a growl and dragging his teeth across those infernal flame-markings just to wipe the smirk off his face.


“Aaahahh!! Get a grip,” Phainon half-whispered, half-hissed, pointing accusingly at the space between his legs. “This is not the time. We’re a prisoner. This is probably the night before an execution! You do not get to be excited right now! You’re supposed to be mourning the plan, not picturing what he’d sound like in bed—argh!”


Phainon whirled in place like it would help him cool off.


“I’m not into bloodstained warmongers with resting murder face and huge chest,” he hissed to himself. “I’m into gentle, quiet types. Like the boy I kissed under a tree. Remember him?”


But Phainon still remembered, vividly that he had landed hits, real ones. He had moved faster than he thought he could, felt the strain in every swing. 


Even when his blade snapped and the crowd roared and his lungs burned, he hadn’t stopped. He hadn’t wanted to stop. Something about Mydei’s fire had lit something deep in him, something primal, stupid, yet addictive.


And Mydeimos had caught him, again and again, with just his bare hands. And cackled. Like a beast who had waited years just for a worthy opponent.


And something in his chest clenched.


“…just the eyes,” he said weakly. “That’s all. Just the eyes. And maybe the hair. And the part where he smiled like he wanted to eat me alive.”


He groaned and dropped to the floor of the balcony, covering his face with both hands.


But the memory returned, Mydeimos cackled in the arena, wild and radiant, blood dripping down his temple as though it were paint on a masterpiece.


That grin.


Those teeth.


And that moment when he caught Phainon mid-swing and murmured something smug under his breath. “That's it. Show me your worst.”


Phainon nearly threw himself off the balcony.


He buried his face in his arms and groaned into the crook of his elbow. “I am going to die. Not from execution. From thirst. I’m going to die as a virgin pervert.”


And his body, traitorous as ever, refusing to forget the shape of that war-born mouth.


"Heh."


Phainon jolted upright, nearly slamming his knee into the balcony rail as a low chuckle echoed from below.


He scrambled toward the edge, peering down, only for his breath to catch in his throat.


There, standing casually in the moonlit courtyard, was Mydeimos.


Head tilted slightly, arms crossed over his bare chest, and those golden eyes, so bright even in the dark, gazing directly up at him.


Phainon’s soul left his body.


“W, What the...! How long have you been standing there?” he called out, almost like a squeak.


Mydeimos shrugged, slow and elegant. “Long enough,” he said. “This is my palace. I can walk where I please, can’t I?”


Phainon tried to laugh. It came out strained. “Right. Of course. That makes sense.”


( Please tell me he didn’t hear me scold my own dick... )


Mydeimos didn’t say anything else at first. Just stood there, his gaze lazily tracking Phainon like a lion half-heartedly considering the effort of pouncing.


Then he raised a brow and asked, “Are all people in Aedes Elysiae as loud as you?”


Phainon blinked, still flustered. “Loud? Me? Nah, I’m just... naturally expressive!”


He threw his arms up in a helpless sort of shrug, trying not to think about how almost seen-through the fabric of Mydeimos' pale golden night robe looked under moonlight. Phainon could swear he could see the silhouette of Mydeimos' red lines on his bare skin.


Meanwhile, the king himself just shrugged. “Right. Of course.”


He turned, as if to walk off.


And maybe that should’ve been the end of it. Phainon could’ve gone back to pacing and scolding himself and pretending he wasn’t seconds away from dreaming about biting Kremnos’s war king.


But something stopped him.


Something in the angle of Mydeimos’s shoulders. The tension in his gait. The way his cloak, loose around one shoulder, dragged behind like it weighed more than it should. It wasn’t much. But Phainon had always been good at reading people, especially the ones who tried hard not to be read.


And Mydeimos… looked alone.


( He always walks like the world belongs to him,) Phainon thought. ( But he never walks with anyone. )


Before he could talk himself out of it, Phainon backed up two steps then jumped.


He leapt clean over the balcony rail, the wind slapping his face as the ground rushed up.


“What—?!”


Mydeimos’s voice cracked for the first time in forever.


He moved fast, half-pivoting, half-lunging, arms instinctively coming up in a defensive stance, as if he thought Phainon was launching an aerial attack.


Phainon landed in a crouch, one foot skidding as he absorbed the impact. His calves screamed in protest. His knees hated him. His spine filed an official complaint.


But he grinned up at Mydeimos anyway.


“Relax. Not here to assassinate you,” he said, raising both hands in surrender.


Mydeimos stared.


“You jumped off a third-floor balcony,” he said flatly.


Phainon dusted off his tunic. “Didn’t really think about it. You just... looked kind of sad standing there by yourself.”


That earned him a look. Not anger. Not amusement either. Just a long, unreadable silence from Mydeimos, as if he were trying to make sense of the sentence.


“I’m not sad.” the king finally muttered, glancing away.


“You sure?” Phainon lingered beside him beneath the moonlight and wincing at the bruises blooming beneath the fabric. "Then, how are you feeling now?"


Mydeimos didn’t answer right away. He turned slightly, enough that the profile of his face caught the light. His brows furrowed, not in anger, but in confusion.


Phainon continued, undeterred. “I mean... I only got hit by your fists. A lot. But you were stabbed. Multiple times. Pretty sure my sword clipped something important near the end.”


Mydeimos scoffed, dryly. “Are you always this concerned about people who try to kill you?”


Phainon shrugged. “Just asking.”


Golden eyes narrowed. For a moment, it looked like Mydeimos might brush it off with one of his usual cold dismissals. But instead, he turned his gaze back to the garden path, letting the silence stretch again.


“I’m used to it,” he said finally. “Mostly healed already.”


Phainon blinked. “What, just like that?”


“I am immortal,” Mydeimos replied, as though it were the most mundane fact in the world. “Wounds close faster. Bones knit overnight. No blade’s ever stayed in long enough to matter.”


“But…” Phainon hesitated, then stepped closer, peering up at the faint smudge of dried blood near Mydeimos’s waist line. “Even if it heals fast, doesn’t it still hurt?”


That question hung in the air.


Simple. Honest.


The kind that could only come from someone too soft-hearted for a world like Kremnos.


Mydeimos met those clear, stubbornly , foolishly sincere eyes.


Phainon didn’t flinch.


And that, perhaps, was what cracked something.


Mydeimos exhaled, slow. His lashes dipped for a second, shadowing the gold.


“…It only hurts,” he murmured, “when I care enough to feel it.”


The answer wasn’t loud. It wasn’t meant to be. But it landed like a stone in a still pond.


Phainon didn’t speak right away. He couldn’t.


There was something hollow and heavy in that sentence. Like an old wound too deep to ever bleed again. He wanted to ask more. About why Mydeimos had stopped caring. About whether the numbness was strength or survival. But he held his tongue. He doubted he was at the right place to be concerned, even though he couldn't really hide it well.


“Right.” Phainon shifted his weight, then smiled faintly. “Well, for what it’s worth… if I stabbed you again tomorrow, I’d definitely care enough to worry about it.”


Mydeimos glanced at him, that faint ghost of a smile tugging briefly at the corner of his mouth.


“You’d have to survive long enough to try.”


Phainon grinned. “Well, a man could hope he'd survive. After all, he wasn't immediately executed and his entire country was spared for ten years out of what he hope is goodwill and not... boredom.”


“That was not boredom.”


“Then mercy?”


“There's no 'mercy' in Kremnoan.”


“Then, a soft spot for cross-dressing farm boy who challenge king to fistfights?”


Mydeimos looked at him, mouth twitching just slightly at the corner.


“Definitely not that.”


"Hmm, how mysterious."


The courtyard was quiet save for the chirping of insects, the rustling of leaves in the distant gardens, and the occasional creak of a torch bracket catching the breeze. Phainon shifted on his feet, every inch of him still sore from the fight, but too curious, and too wired, to go back to his room.


He glanced at Mydeimos again, unwilling to end the talk. “Do you always wander around your palace at night?”


“Do you always throw yourself off balconies?”


“Only when I see someone who looks like they need a friend.”


That made something flicker in Mydeimos’s expression. It was subtle, so subtle most wouldn’t notice, but to someone like Phainon, who’d grown up watching storms roll across the valley just by how the clouds tilted, it was obvious.


A crack in the armor.


Then Mydeimos took a step away and said, “You should get some rest. Unlike me, you're very much mortal, even if you're slightly deranged."


Phainon watched him for a moment more. The moonlight painted his gold markings like they were glowing. Even now, post-battle, half-dressed and scowling, the man looked more like a painting than a person. Definitely not like how the rumours had pictured him to.


"Are you worried about me, Your Majesty?”


Mydeimos didn’t stop, didn’t turn, but his pace faltered for half a step. A pause, subtle, like a breath caught in his throat. Then, with a nonchalant shrug of one shoulder, he answered nothing.


Phainon laughed, the sound light and teasing. “That was definitely a yes.”


Still no response.


“And here I thought you wanted me executed.” Phainon tilted his head, adopting a thoughtful expression. “But now you’re telling me to sleep, worrying about me. That's such a mixed signals.”


At that, the golden-eyed king turned just slightly, enough for moonlight to catch the sharp lines of his jaw. His expression clearly judging Phainon's sanity now.


But Phainon decided to ignore it, leaned against the nearest column, his tone laced with mock innocence. “Y’know, I did arrive here as a bride. Veil and all. If you’re have no intention to kill me, why not go through with the marriage instead?”


Now, Mydeimos turned fully. His head was tilted, eyebrows knitted so close, marred his beautifulf feature.


“I’m sure Kremnoans would approve,” Phainon added, gesturing to his own bruised arms. “They seemed pretty smitten with my figure. I mean, I’ve got strong calves and a decent smile. That counts, right? Strong brides seem to be in fashion here.”


Mydeimos scoffed, folding his arms. “Would you marry someone even if you felt nothing for them? Even if it was just politics?”


The question had a blade under it. Not mocking. Not quite serious either. Just sharp enough to draw thought.


“Well…” He looked up toward the stars, absently scratching the back of his neck. “I’m just a farm boy, really. Raised with wheat fields, not diplomacy. Never had a throne or a war to think about.”


He smiled a little, more to himself than anyone else.


“But yeah,” he admitted quietly. “I guess I would.”


 Wind stirred the garden trees as Mydeimos shook his head.


"Don't you have someone waiting home? LIke the princess you protected 'till you bleed and bruised."


“Cyrene? Haha, no. She is more like a sister to me.” Phainon, looked away for the first time, glancing up to the sky above. “Though, yeah. I have someone. I am the one who wait for him to return. This scrawny little kid with wild hair and big gold eyes. Seems like he's in big trouble, always looked so alerted. Looked like a kitten who stumbled into the wrong barn. But, he was the most beautiful person I've ever seen. Got stuck in my head for years.”


Phainon’s voice softened with the memory which replayed in his mind.


“He was scrappy. Fast. He liked climbing places just to look at the sky. He hid from everything, but when he smiled, it was like he hadn’t been hurt yet.” His tone was heavy with fondness, so was his smile. “I told him I’d wait for him no matter how long. Still planning to.”


Then he huffed and shook his head. “But I have a land to protect. If my future’s the price… then so be it.”


Silence lingered between them. From the corner of his eye, Phainon saw Mydeimos’s face shift ever so slightly as he looked away. Not in scorn. Not in amusement.


His ears were a little pink.


It was so brief, so faint, Phainon almost thought he imagined it. Probably the lanterns, or the moon, or the way shadows curved under bone.


But before Phainon could say anything, Mydeimos turned fully around, face set back into his usual blank mask.


“You’re starting to sound like someone delirious.”


Phainon barked a laugh. “I do have a head injury.”


Mydeimos already turned away again, retreating back into the palace with long, quiet strides.


Phainon called after him, a grin breaking across his face. “I was joking, mostly! But hey, the offer stands. Just so you know, I prefer to get married than to die.”


Mydeimos paused in the distance. Then, he raised a hand over his shoulder without looking back. Whether it was a gesture of dismissal or acknowledgment, Phainon couldn’t tell.


But tonight, the ruthless king seemed a little more human to him.

**

chapters.title: The Price for Freedom
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

tw: Phainon's wet dream lol

Phainon woke with a gasp.


His sheets were twisted around his legs, damp with sweat. The morning light filtering through the carved stone window felt too warm, too golden, like it was mocking him.


His chest heaved.


“...Oh, wow,” he whispered, dragging both hands over his face.


The dream still clung to him like mist.


It hadn’t been a violent one. Not like the clash of swords or thunderous shouts from the colosseum. No, this had been quiet. Intimate. Slow in a way that made it far worse.


He remembered the scent first, a faint trace of something sweet on his breath. And then the weight. The warmth.


In the dream, Mydeimos had straddled him.


Not with cruelty. Not like a conqueror. But with something heavy and raw in his golden eyes, as if he wanted, needed to be so close.


His thighs bracketed Phainon’s hips, his palms pressed flat against Phainon’s chest, holding him there, grounding him. His red-marked skin gleamed in the dim light, smooth and impossibly warm under touch. His hair was damp, curling slightly where it brushed Phainon’s collarbone. And his expression…


It hadn’t been smug.


Not entirely.


Phainon saw a flicker of hunger laced with wariness. Like he was offering something no one had dared ask of him before. Being held, riding out whatever storm was brewing between them like they meant more than it should’ve.


Mydeimos had moved slowly. Testing him. As if teasing his self-restraint.


But dream-Phainon was not hesitating.


He’d reached up, his palm landed on his chest, the fingers made a playful twirl around the nipple, forcing Mydeimos to arch his back, moaning so sweetly, smiling so devilishly.


And then, Mydeimos started to dance, a maddening rhythm, bouncing. His lips were trembling when he called out Phainon's name.


"ARGHHH!!" Phainon groaned into his pillow now, mortified, burying his face so deep into it he nearly smothered.


“What is wrong with me…”


His lower half twitched in protest, the memory of pressure and warmth refusing to fade. He grit his teeth, yanking the blanket up to his waist, then yanking it right back down when it made everything worse.


He lay there, fists clenched in his sheets, trying to will the image away.


( Mydeimos. Of all people. )


Phainon flushed deeper and stared miserably at the canopy above him.


Then, worst of all, he felt the heat pooling again. The sharp thrum of arousal that had yet to leave him.


He smacked a hand over his groin like he was scolding a misbehaving animal. “Stop it,” he hissed. “Don't force me to betray my kitty cat."


His body disagreed.


With every heartbeat, the dream replayed in his mind like intrusive thought. Mydei’s hips, the sound of breathless chuckles near his ear, the scrape of his thigh across Phainon’s waist. That moment where he had leaned in too close and whispered...


A sharp knock at the door made him bolt upright.


Three knocks. Clean. Formal.


Phainon panicked, twisting his blanket over his lap. “O-one moment!”


The door opened anyway.


Three palace attendants entered with practiced grace, ignoring the mess of sheets and flushed farmboy. They bowed in near-unison.


“The King has summoned you,” one said, eyes politely downcast.


Phainon blinked, still breathless. “Summoned? Already?”


“You are to be prepared for audience.”


“I, I need to clean myself first!” he blurted, cracking. “Please. Just. Just give me a second!”


The attendants exchanged no glances. One gestured toward the adjoining bath chamber. “The tub is drawn. We shall ready your garments.”


Phainon stumbled toward the bath, his dignity left behind on the mattress.


The moment he slipped into the steaming water, he exhaled sharply, pressing a hand to his still-burning face. His skin stung as the water touched the half-healed cuts on his arms. Another attendant entered to reapply the balm to his wounds, silent and efficient.


Phainon let his head fall back.


As the attendants entered again to tend to his wounds and offer garments of formal wear, Phainon dried himself off with a sigh.


He tugged on a deep sapphire tunic trimmed in silver and fastened his belt, all the while wondering what kind of summons this would be.


( Execution in velvet? A lecture about diplomatic trickery? )


Honestly, at this point, anything was possible.


But one thing was certain.


If he saw Mydeimos today and that stupid dream so much as flickered behind his eyes again…


He might need to throw himself into the nearest fountain.


After trying to get ahold of himself (and his libido), Phainon was escorted by some guards. This time, they didn’t lead Phainon back to the great hall.


Instead, they took a different corridor, less grand, quieter, lined with rows of busts and dark velvet curtains. The air smelled faintly of paper, wax, and metal ink. There was no gold, no pomp, no sword-lined walls. Just silence, punctuated by the soft shuffle of boots on marble.


A knight knocked the door and Krateros opened a tall oak door.


"Please, come in. Our king is waiting inside."


Phainon gulped and nodded, dragging his steps inside.

The room beyond was... a study.


Not what he’d expected from the feared king of Kremnos.


It was tall and shadowed, half-lit by angled skylights. Bookshelves lined every wall, so densely packed that some books were stacked sideways atop others. Scrolls sat in bundles beside stacks of official-looking files, scattered with bookmarks made of ribbon and even, in one case, what looked like a fork. A globe sat in the corner, slightly askew. The fireplace wasn’t lit, but there was a half-empty cup of something warm still steaming on a small side table.


And behind a broad, polished desk at the far end, half-buried beneath a mountain of parchment, sat Mydeimos.


Phainon’s breath hitched.


He didn’t gasp aloud, but almost, so close.


The king was reading a report, head tilted down, quill tapping absently against the desk. His crimson cloak was nowhere to be seen, replaced with a black high-collared shirt rolled to the elbows, revealing familiar red markings curling along his arms. His hair was loosely tied back, just enough to keep it out of his face.


And perched perfectly on the bridge of his nose, glasses.


Thin-framed. Gold-rimmed. Dangerously attractive.


But truly, Mydeimos looked so handsome like that. Less like a tyrant, more like a noble professor who could make laws and ruin reputations with a single note. 


Phainon sat down automatically when Krateros gestured to the set of chairs near the corner, sofa on one side, single chair on the other, a low table between them. It felt like a reception area, something that belonged to a minister, not a warlord. He couldn't help but to keep looking, staring at Mydeimos as he waited.


Time passed in slow minutes. Mydeimos continued signing and stamping documents. Occasionally, he ripped one in half without even looking up, letting the parchment fall into a brass bin beside him. Every so often, he adjusted his glasses with a single finger, brows drawn in silent judgment at whatever poor soul had sent him a report so unsatisfactory.


Phainon didn’t know why, but he felt... tense.


His palms itched. He could still feel the way Mydeimos had moved in the arena, that brutal elegance. And now, now he was just a man in glasses, working through paperwork, and somehow that made him even harder to look away from.


Finally, Mydeimos set his quill down and stood.


He didn’t speak immediately. He walked, unhurried, to where Phainon sat and extended a single sheet of paper.


Phainon blinked up at him.


“Sign this,” Mydeimos said simply.


Phainon took the paper with both hands, expecting another death warrant or a list of demands.


What he found instead nearly made his heart seize.


The parchment was thick, official. Stamped already with Kremnos’s seal, its crimson wax still fresh and glinting. At the top, in curling gold-lettered script:


“Union Pact of Accord and Matrimony.”


His eyes dropped lower, skimming lines faster now.


His name. Written clearly. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. Everything filled out, birth date, parental lineage, witness fields, all meticulously prepared.


Only one blank space remained.


The signature line on his side.


His gaze drifted left.


The opposing name was already signed.


Mydeimos of Kremnos.


The red ink of his name curled like a cut into the parchment. Sharp, unmistakable.


Phainon stared at it in disbelief, then flicked his eyes up to the man behind the desk.


“You’re,” His voice broke in surprise. “You’re serious?”


Mydeimos, still wearing those glasses, didn’t blink. “Do I look like someone who jokes in moments like this?”


Phainon opened his mouth. Then closed it. Then opened it again to say, “I, This isn’t how it’s supposed to go. You’re supposed to, I don’t know, throw me in prison. Public execution. Burn the veil.”


“You said you came as a bride, didn’t you?” he said, deadpan. “I’m simply honoring the diplomatic gesture.”


Phainon opened his mouth, closed it, then opened it again. “That was—! I was joking! Well, mostly.”


“You also challenged me to a duel,” Mydeimos replied.


“That makes me your rival, or someone foolish!”


"No, actually that makes you my bride.'


"Huhhh?!"


Mydeimos glanced at Krateros.


“Remind me,” he said calmly, “how did my parents meet?”


Krateros, without even lifting his head from the ledger he’d been sorting through in the corner, replied smoothly, "The late queen challenged the late king for duel. They fought. Equal strength. The king promised the throne for anyone who bested him. But since no one losing, he proposed to the queen. She threw a spear through his shoulder as answer. Then, they were married by dusk. Since then, many followed their steps to find spouses.”


Mydeimos raised a brow and looked back at Phainon.


The expression on his face was devastatingly smug, a smirk that told Phainon that it was normalcy here.


Phainon blinked. “You’re saying fighting to death is... traditional courtship?!”


“I’m saying that you should've learn about the local tradition before you challenged their king. Alas, you survived ten days in the Colosseum,” Mydeimos said, sliding the paper closer to him. “You fought me to a standstill and that's the best proposal I ever received.”


“But I lied to you.”


“You fought me.”


“I wore a dress.”


“You fought me well.”


Phainon pressed the heel of his palm against his forehead, exasperated, then running both hands through his hair. He stared at the ceiling like it might open up and offer him some divine insight, or maybe an escape route.


Instead, all he got was a quill offered to him.


“Let me get this straight,” Phainon said slowly. “You’re not going to kill me.”


“Correct.”


“You’re not going to send me home if I refuse?”


“No. you’ll be imprisoned.”


Phainon’s brows lifted. “So much for mercy.”


“There is no 'mercy' here, I told you before. Besides, you tried to deceive the Kingdom of Kremnos,” Mydeimos said, still maddeningly calm. “Under false identity. Infiltrated my court. Lied to my face. I'd be well within my rights to call it threat."


“Right." Phainon grunted. "And you’re proposing.”


“You proposed, I’ve already signed.” Mydeimos shrugged with all the grace of someone utterly unbothered. “I recall you said you'd rather get married than die."


"Right, but..." Phainon stared at him. “You're about to marry someone who lied, cross-dressed, challenged you in public, insulted your politics, and broke your nose.”


“You didn’t break my nose.”


“I tried. But, you know, there's nothing you'll get from this marriage. I'm just a farm boy with nothing to offer."


"True, for another place, maybe." Mydeimos folded his arms. "But you're in Kremnos. We value strength over anything else. You are worthy."


"Are you sure, to do this?"


"Stop questioning me and sign already." Mydeimos once again shoved the quill closer, getting impatient.


Phainon swallowed, then heaving a very tired sigh.


There was no clever route out. This was the end of the road.


And at that end stood a ridiculous choice: a cell, or a crown.


( And people thought sheep herding was hard... )


“…Fine,” he muttered, grabbing the quill. He signed it with a scratch of ink, slanted and rushed. The last loop of his name ended with a flourish that looked more like a desperate sigh than calligraphy.


He let the quill drop, rubbing his temple with a groan. “This is the most unromantic marriage proposal in history.”


Mydeimos arched one perfect brow. “You're still alive. That’s more romance than most get from me.”


“Touché,” Phainon muttered.


Mydeimos rolled the parchment up, stamped it with the seal of finality, and gave it to Krateros for further preparation. Then he stood, brushing his fingers off like he had just finalized a grain trade.


"You'll be returning to Aedes Elysiae once your wounds are healed. I'll dismiss your envoys to bring the news. The royal knights will do the escort for you later,” he said. “You’ll return to pack your things. Settle your affairs. Come back here in three days.”


Phainon blinked. “Huh? Why?!”


“You’ll be moving in, of course,” Mydeimos said, like it was obvious. “You are now the queen of Kremnos.”


The room tilted slightly.


Phainon’s jaw dropped.


“I, what, I'm a queen just because I just signed the paper?!"

"You married the king, it's obvious you're the queen now."

"Won't people, or err, the nobles revolt on a nobody being their queen?!"

"Do you think anyone in this kingdom brave enough to question my authority?"

"Right, of course." Phainon grunted, he didn't think it through when he said everything last night. "At least, let me breath a bit!”


Mydeimos didn't wait for Phainon to collect his thought and instead just raised his fingers. "You can breath during your recovery and in those three days in your hometown. Say good bye to your family. Be glad. At least, as the hometown of our Queen, Aedes Elysiae will be protected under Kremnos' flag."


Phainon groaned into his hands. “What in the name of Titans did I just get myself into…”

**

chapters.title: Home Sweet Home
chapters.html:
Phainon adjusted the cloak draped over his shoulders as the carriage rolled through the gate.

Despite the velvet wrapping and the sunlight flooding through the windows, a strange chill settled in his bones. 

It had been a week since he signed that ridiculous paper with trembling fingers. Seven full days in the palace of Kremnos. And despite the opulence, the warm baths, the fruits arranged into flowers on every tray… Phainon had never felt more unsure of what he was.

He could feel the shift in air, the thick tension of departure, the distant thrum of horns sounding his leave. Beyond the window, Kremnos bathed in its usual dusty gold, brilliant and intimidating, with walls carved like scars and banners of crimson flickering against the wind.

The people were already out.

Crowds had formed by the sides of the road, murmuring, bowing, calling out things that made Phainon’s ears warm despite himself.

“There she is, our Queen!”

“No, no, that’s a he. Didn’t you hear? It’s a man!”

“Man or not, the Queen fought our king for ten days! That’s more queenly than half the court.”

“I saw him tear his skirt mid-fight. Like a goddess of war!”

“Bless the Queen’s thighs. Long live the Queen of Kremnos!”

Phainon choked on his own breath.

Even now, after everything, even after the veil had been burned and he’d walked into the bathhouse shirtless, they still called him Queen. Not mockingly. Not sarcastically. Just… reverently.

Queen.

Like it was a title that had nothing to do with gender.

He’d asked a maid once, after catching her calling him “My Queen” with a curtsy and a grin.

“Do you all really not mind I’m… not exactly what you expected?”

The maid blinked. “You fought His Majesty with a broken sword and lived. Why wouldn’t you be our Queen?”

He hadn’t known what to say to that. Still didn’t.

He pressed his forehead against the cool windowpane, watching the blur of red stone and cheering figures go by.

They didn’t mock him.

They praised him.

They loved him.

Some had even started weaving little braids into their hair, copying the tight plaits Phainon had worn once. The look had been accidental. He’d just gotten bored in the bath and tied his hair up, but apparently it was now fashionable.

One soldier had bowed and called it the braid of battle.

He groaned again into his palm.

This place was unhinged.

And somehow, strangely, it had accepted him in a way nothing else ever had.

A male Queen. A battlefield bride. A ridiculous, veiled warrior in a gown barely stitched to his thighs.

And somehow… that worked here.

It made the quiet in his chest ache a little more.

The part of him that remembered running barefoot with Cyrene through wheat fields. The part that had once dreamed, naively, that he’d meet a boy with amber eyes and kitten-sharp smiles and finally get to love without sacrifice.

Now, here he was, wrapped in royal silk and embroidered lace, being sent home not as a liar or a criminal, but as a consort.

A queen.

“My Queen,” came the knight’s voice from outside. “We’ll cross the border by dusk.”

Phainon leaned back, arms crossed behind his head, his voice was dry with satirical humour.

“I’m a man, you know.”

Silence.

Then a polite cough. “Yes, we're fully aware.”

Phainon sighed. “Of course.”

He couldn’t even be annoyed. Not really.

Maybe this was fine.

He glanced out the window one more time.

Kremnos was nearly behind him now, the spires fading into distance.

But in the pit of his stomach, something turned with a strange, fluttering weight.

The strangest part of everything wasn’t the overly eccentric people.

It was the absence of Mydeimos.

The so-called husband.

In seven days, he’d been summoned three times. Once, to dine in a marble hall lit by golden sconces and studded with enough forks to arm a militia. Mydeimos barely touched his food. Phainon barely touched his nerves. Still, they talked, well, Phaion talked. About the weather. The shape of clouds. A new fruit he discovered in the gardens that stung when bitten.

The second time, another dinner. This time quieter. More comfortable, in a weird, hanging way. Like two people sitting at the edge of a silence they didn’t know how to fill.

And once, Mydeimos visited his chamber.

That moment lingered longer than it should have.

He hadn’t come with guards. Just himself, dressed down in black and gold, eyes scanning Phainon with that unreadable weight.

“You’re healing,” he said, eyes grazing over Phainon’s half-bared shoulder where a bruise had once bloomed.

Phainon raised a brow, trying not to feel stupidly warm. “Yeah. I do that fast. Not as fast as you, fire-marked miracle that you are, but fast enough.”

Mydeimos didn’t smile. Just gave a quiet hum, glanced at the wine tray like he wasn’t sure what to say next, and then left as abruptly as he came.

And somehow… that felt worse than a prison.

Because wasn’t marriage supposed to be something else?

Something more than title and silence?

Phainon had never dreamed of weddings or thrones. He was a field boy who learned to fight to survive, not to conquer. He didn’t mind hardship. He minded... loneliness.

“Some king,” Phainon muttered, scowling out the carriage window. “Marries a guy, then vanishes like mist.”

He tilted his head, watching the land blur by, then added under his breath, “Does he even remember marrying me?”

His grumbling didn’t fool himself. Not really. Because with every petty jab, his visage softened just a little, turned more wistful, more bitten-off at the end.

He expected at least a goodbye when he departed.

Or a wave.

Or maybe his judgemental glare.

But there was nothing.

No golden-haired brute to scowl at him from the battlements. No silent, awkward escort to the gate. Just the royal guard, the carriage, and the low buzz of civilians still praising him in the distance.

Phainon sighed, letting his head tip back.

“Guess I’m the only one who remembers the wedding,” he mumbled. “That’s fine. I didn’t cry or anything. Didn’t even get a cake. Or a kiss. Some honeymoon.”

He let the sulk settle into his bones a little deeper, staring at the shifting sky as the sun climbed steadily above.

It wasn’t like he’d wanted a real marriage. He just… expected something from his husband. Maybe a fraction of attention like he got from his people. Or, anything. Even a parting insult. Mydeimos, for all his fire and fury, had grown cold in the aftermath. As if naming Phainon queen was just a matter of record, not... something personal.

“Maybe it wasn’t personal,” he murmured. “It's politic, right? Hah, it doesn't like we get married because we love each other or something.”

His voice was smaller now, tight with pain around the edges.

He looked down at his lap, at the fine gloves covering his fingers, at the soft cloth draped over bruises already fading too fast. He healed quickly. Faster than most. It wasn’t fair.

He could’ve used a little more time to ache.

He glanced once more behind him, but the towers of Kremnos were gone now, devoured by cliffs and fog.

A hollow ache bloomed behind his ribs.

His thoughts tangled like roots.

Cyrene must’ve heard already. Or would soon. His name would’ve reached every corner of Amphoreus by now, carried on the tongues of the envoys and merchants.

They’d say he fought for his homeland's peace.

But had Mydeimos told them they got married? Did the people back home even know?

Would Cyrene laugh at him? Or cry? Would she still call him her hero?

He rubbed his forehead, groaning softly.

His fingers curled slightly against the window glass, his voice was barely a murmur.

“Still miss you, y’know.”

He meant the boy from all those years ago. That scruffy little stray who had wandered into his childhood like a secret. All fire eyes and startled-cat silence. All rough elbows and skittish frowns. The one Phainon had been waiting for. Hoping for.

His ears burned. His heart ached.

But mostly, he just felt… stupid.

And a little lonely.

“Some reunion that would be,” he chuckled dryly. “If I ever meet him again, I’ll just tell him I accidentally married someone else while saving the world. I’m sure he’ll understand.”

The carriage bearing the sun-eater lion, the emblazoned crest of Kremnos rolled into Aedes Elysiae like a storm cloud on a clear day. Its polished frame glinted gold in the sunlight, an uneasy contrast against the cobbled streets and soft pastel homes of the humble kingdom. People paused mid-step, turning, staring, murmuring.

"A Kremnoan royal carriage?"

"Here?"

Some began to gather along the road, cautious, curious, whispering questions. Had they come to demand something again? Was it war? Another tribute?

Then the carriage slowed by the central square. The horses stilled. The door swung open.

And from it leapt someone tall and familiar, unmistakable even through the expensive looking garb.

“Phainon...?”

A breathless voice broke the silence.

Then someone cried his name.

And then another.

Soon the air was full of it.

“Phainon! He’s back!”

They rushed toward him. Children from the farms, stallkeepers with flour-dusted hands, elders leaning on walking sticks. He had been one of their best; bright, strong, reckless, warm like sunlight. And now he was here, alive, stepping out from a Kremnos carriage like the punchline of a divine joke.

He barely had time to smile before someone else screamed: “Get Audata!” and the crowd parted like wheat before a gust of wind.

His mother came flying.

Audata had always been proud. The kind of woman who moved with purpose and never raised her voice unless she meant to shake the skies. But now? She was barefoot, apron half-tied, tears streaking her cheeks as she ran.

Phainon barely had time to open his arms before she slammed into him, wrapping him tight, sobbing against his chest.

“You idiot,” she breathed between hiccups. “You stupid, reckless boy. You’re alive.”

His father, Hieronymus, arrived seconds later, slower, but just as fierce. He gripped Phainon’s shoulder with a hand calloused from decades of harvest, then yanked him into a tighter hug, one arm wrapping around Audata as they stood together, all three clinging to each other like the world might still take him away.

“You’ve lost weight,” Phainon said, blinking past his own misting vision.

“So have you,” Hieronymus grunted. “War suits no one.”

“I wasn’t at war.”

“You fought the King of Kremnos for days,” Audata snapped, pulling back to squint at him. “You were at war.”

The mention of it seemed to spark a hundred questions. But Phainon only smiled, gently pried his mother’s fingers from his arm, and said, “Let’s go home.”

Before he left, he asked the captain of royal knight where they would stay. Apparently, the Kremnoan knights already decided to stay on guard at the edge of the village, camped quietly and respectfully, clearly briefed on Aedes Elysiae hospitality and the sacredness of its harvest. The square didn’t have space for them, nor the inn, and besides, no one here wanted armed strangers too close to their fields.

Phainon thanked them before he went with his parents, waving his hands at every people who greeted him.

Their house hadn’t changed. It still stood at the edge of the village, nestled between a slope of old fig trees and the lazy brook that hadn’t once dried in Phainon’s memory. The wooden shutters were still crooked. The roof still wore moss like a crown. It smelled like cumin and dirt and the soft familiar scent of growing things.

Inside the house, Phainon sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with a cracked bowl of soup cooling beside him while his parents buzzed around with alternating moods of scolding, pride, and disbelief.

“You could’ve died,” Audata muttered, wiping a stubborn spot on the table for the fifth time. 

“Then, is it true?” Hieronymus asked, stirring the hearth. “Did you challenge the King?”

“Ten days,” Audata whispered again. “They said you fought him for ten days and nights. Your body, how are you even walking?”

“You know,” Phainon replied with a shrug. “I'm fine now. I'm always a fast healer.”

“You’re still reckless,” his mother sniffed, sitting beside him and placing a hand on his cheek. “You were always running off for others, never thinking of yourself.”

“I thought about you,” Phainon murmured. “That’s why I fought.”

Hieronymus made a sound of approval, placing a plate of bread in front of him.

“And now you’re home,” he said, resting a hand on his son’s shoulder. “In time for harvest. The barley’s strong this year. Three more months, and we’ll be feasting.”

“Three months,” Phainon echoed softly.

It should’ve made him happy. But a cold curl had begun to form in his gut.

Because as they smiled and spoke of feast and seed and blessed rains, he realized something, they didn’t know.

They didn’t know he was married.

Not just married, but becoming a queen.

Phainon’s gaze dropped to his untouched soup, to the golden cuff still wrapped around his wrist, the one with Kremnos insignia. No one had questioned it. No one even noticed.

The warmth of home, the simple joy of soup and laughter, all dulled into the background as Phainon’s smile began to slip.


Just slightly. Just enough for Audata to notice.


She reached out, fingers brushing his arm. “Phai? What is it?”


Hieronymus set his bowl down, squinting. “You look like you’re carrying a stone in your chest.”


Phainon looked between them, at his mother’s soft concern, his father’s quiet strength, and something in his chest twisted.


He lowered his gaze.


And bowed.


Low. Deep. Until his forehead almost touched his knee.


“I’m sorry,” he said barely above a whisper. “I can’t help with the harvest this year.”


Audata blinked, taken aback. “What? What do you mean you can’t?”


“I… I want to,” he said, lifting his head with a sheepish grin. “But, well… I got married.”


There was a beat of stunned stillness.


Then Audata let out a sharp exhale, eyes wide. “Married?”


Hieronymus brow knitting, as if he hadn’t heard right.


Phainon rubbed the back of his neck, trying for a laugh. “Yeah. Unexpectedly. In Kremnos.”


They exchanged a glance, a flash of shock between them, but quickly forced smiles onto their faces.


“Oh, well,” Hieronymus said, clearing his throat. “Then of course you’d have to stay with your… your spouse. That’s unexpected but we understand.”


“Oh, yes, yes,” Audata said, still reeling. “We’ll visit when we can. What’s her name? Is she with you? Did she stay at the camp?”


Phainon’s throat tightened.


He took a breath. And then, he dropped the truth carefully. “I married the king.”


But the words landed with the weight of thunder.


Silence fell. Not the soft kind, but the brittle, shattering sort.


Audata’s smile cracked.


Hieronymus stared at him like his son had just spoken in a language no one taught them.


“The… the king?” Audata echoed, slowly.


“Of Kremnos,” Phainon added, weaker now. “Mydeimos.”


“Phainon, it's not funny.” His father’s voice was low and sharp.


Phainon flinched, but he kept his smile. The corner of his lips twitched. The couple knew it well, their son was talking the truth.


The blood drained from Hieronymus’ face. Audata’s fingers trembled where they gripped her apron.


“You married… that tyrant?”


“He’s not, well,” Phainon faltered. “He’s intense, yeah, but it’s not like he's absolutely cruel too. After the duel, he gave me a choice, either to get imprisoned or… marry him.”


"But why?" Audata's lips quivered the question.


"Ahaha, I kinda, err, made him mad?" His grin was brittle, glass-thin. “And, well… I figured marriage wasn’t the worst. At least now, Aedes Elysiae won’t have to give tributes. The kingdom’s under protection, no more taxes, no more fear.”


He tried to sound proud. Triumphant, even.


But his voice cracked on the last word.


Audata was shaking her head, slowly, as if trying to wake up. “Phai… You married into Kremnos. The very hands that took our fields. You...”


“I know,” he cut in quietly. “I know. And if I could’ve found another way, I would’ve.”


He looked down again, gripping his knees. “I could just chose the prison but our people might stay suffered later. I chose the marriage so our people could sleep without checking the borders every week.”


A pause.


And suddenly, his mother was hugging him again. Tighter than before.


“You fought so well,” she whispered, voice was clouded with tears. “You foolish, wonderful boy.”


Hieronymus knelt beside them, one large hand resting on Phainon’s head, warm and firm. “You never fail to make us proud.”


Phainon squeezed his eyes shut, swallowing the lump in his throat. His parents didn’t cheer. They didn’t pretend this was happy news.


But they held him.


And in their arms, even without their full understanding, he knew they loved him still.


Dinner passed with warm soup and fresh bread, the same menu that his mother always made on days that needed comfort. They didn’t speak much about the future, only about the land, the fishes, and how the eastern orchard had finally started to bear peaches again. Phainon let the conversation wash over him, chiming in with soft laughter where he could, but mostly just listening, drinking in the sound of home.


Later, he laid on his old straw mattress with the clean scent of the family hearth drifting in through the cracks in the shutters. His body, though still aching faintly, sank into the bedding with a strange heaviness—not just exhaustion, but something deeper.


Peace.


He hadn’t felt this way in a long time. Not in the palace with velvet sheets and perfumed water. Not in the quiet corridors of Kremnos. And certainly not in the battle that lasted ten nights and ten days.


Here, with the faint crackling of firewood, his parents just a room away, and the scent of roasted roots still lingering in the air, this felt real.


He fell asleep quickly.


But sometime in the stillness of night, his eyes fluttered open.


Not from pain. Not from a nightmare.


But from the sound of quiet sobs.


He didn’t move. His breath stayed slow, shallow. He kept his eyes closed, pretending to still sleep.


His mother’s voice was barely above a whisper, thick with grief. “Hieronymus… What if this will be the last time we see him?”


There was a pause. Then the low rumble of his father’s voice. “Don’t say that.”


“But what if it is?” she whispered. “He… He looked thinner. Maybe there are scars behind his clothes.”


Phainon bit the inside of his cheek. He kept still.


“We could visit,” his father said gently. “Maybe not the palace itself, but we’ll hear of him. From the town, from the traveling merchants. We’ll write, and one day—”


“He’ll write back?” Audata’s voice cracked. “Even if he does, what if he can’t say the truth? What if they’re watching? What if they hurt him and we wouldn’t even know?”


Her voice trembled. “That kingdom… it’s cruel. Kremnos has always been cruel. The last queen died by the king’s own hand. And this one... He killed his own father for the throne. A tyrant’s son, raised on blood and power. And now our boy…”


Phainon clenched his fists beneath the blanket.


“I know,” Hieronymus murmured. “I’ve heard the same.”


A pause.


“But Audata… He chose this.”


His mother wept harder at that.


“He did it to save us,” Hieronymus went on. “To protect Aedes Elysiae. To buy our peace. He gave up his own future, maybe even his life, so others could have theirs. What kind of courage does that take?”


His voice was firm, but still so soft to touch the heart of a mother.


“And if that’s the path he chose… the least we can do is honour it. Not with tears. Not with dread. But by standing tall, the way he did.”


Audata’s sobs slowed into trembling breaths.


“I’ll try. But only after tonight.” She sniffled.  “I just, he’s my child. I raised him with lullabies, taught him kindness. He used to cry over scraped knees. He used to dance when the goats followed him, running through the fields, laughing so happily...”


Her voice cracked again. “Why must the fate be so cruel to him? Why those Kremnoan take my baby away from me?” And then, even softer: “Phai… Oh my sweet child…”


Phainon’s tears had already slipped from his lashes.


He didn’t move. Didn’t breathe too deeply. He lay curled under his blanket like a child again, but the guilt in his chest was older than anything he'd ever carried before.


He wanted to reach out. To tell them it was alright. That Mydeimos hadn’t hurt him. That maybe… maybe he was far better than the rumors.


But he didn’t.


Because they were grieving in the only way they could. And pretending to sleep, pretending to be untouched, was his way of honouring them back.


Of giving them this one night.


Of carrying his own pain alone, just a little longer.

The next morning, Phainon rose with the dawn. He pretended not to notice his parents’ red-rimmed eyes or how his mother avoided looking at him too long. Instead, he greeted them with his usual grin and rolled up his sleeves to help with the chores.


There was something comforting about the farm work. Pulling weeds, mending fences, shooing away stubborn goats. It felt like slipping into a well-worn coat. The ache in his limbs from the field was the same kind of ache he remembered as a child, before swords and palaces and ten-day battles. By midday, his arms were dirt-streaked, his hair was a mess, and he laughed so hard at a neighbor’s goat ramming into a tree that he nearly doubled over.


Lunch was simple but comforting. Pickled vegetables, grilled fish, and millet bread with soft cheese. He sat with his parents under the awning of their house, feet bare against the cool dirt, the breeze carrying the scent of citrus and hay.


And then, came a knock and a familiar voice called, “Phai?”


Phainon blinked and stood, brushing the dirt from his knees. When he opened the gate, he froze.


“Cyrene?”


She stood there, cloak drawn tight, her hood pushed back just enough to reveal flushed cheeks and wind-tousled pinky hair. Her eyes widened the moment she saw him.


“You’re alive,” she whispered.


He laughed. “I should be the one saying that to you. I thought you ran off.”


“I almost did,” she admitted. “But I came back. I couldn’t... I couldn’t run away, not after what you did.”


They walked through the orchard path behind the house, sunlight filtering through the leaves in scattered beams. The citrus trees had begun to bloom again, tiny white flowers perfuming the air.


“You weren’t supposed to come back,” Phainon said, bumping her shoulder with his. “You broke our promise.”


“I know.” Her voice was turning into apologetical whisper. “I’m sorry.”


He let the silence sit for a moment before sighing. “Why?”


Cyrene exhaled slowly. “Because I was scared. And selfish. I did run away. But I kept thinking… if you failed, then they’d come for me anyway. I thought… maybe if I’m here, I can say I’m sorry myself.”


Phainon looked at her, lips tugging into a pout. “I took the blame for you, you know.”


“I know.”


“I fought the king of Kremnos.”


She winced. “I know.”


“In a dress.”


“And so I heard. You even ripped it mid-fight.”


He gave a dramatic sigh, turning away like a betrayed heroine. “Unforgivable.”


Cyrene giggled and tugged his sleeve. “Forgive me?”


Phainon peeked at her through narrowed eyes, before grinning. “Fine. Just this once.”


They walked on for a while, the leaves rustling above them.


After a while, Cyrene said, “I told them the moment I returned.”


“Told who?”


“Everyone. The elders. The council. Your parents.” She hesitated. “I told them you chose to fight. That you offered yourself for Aedes Elysiae. That I had no right to stop you. When the envoys returned, we matched our stories to the very small detail.”


“So everyone knew?”


“They knew you were detained,” she clarified. “That you fought, that you… saved us. Ten years of freedom. Enough time to rebuild.”


“But not the marriage.”


Cyrene shook her head. “I didn’t say anything. I thought… that should come from you.”


He stopped walking, staring ahead. “So they only know I’m a hero.”


She nodded. “A hero. Not a bride.”


Phainon let out a soft laugh, tilting his head back to stare at the sky. “Well, that’s one thing I didn’t expect to be in my life story.”


Cyrene looked at him, her voice softer now. “You saved our home.”


Phainon grinned, shaking his head. "I just did what I can."


"Maybe, but it's nothing easy." Cyrene held out his hand, grasped Phainon's in hers. And when she smiled at him, there was guilt and gratitude woven together. “Thank you for everything, Phainon.”


He squeezed her hand back. “Don’t make me do it again.”


"Of course, except when there's another warlord looking for a wife...?" Cyrene winked, playfully.


They both laughed, and for a moment, the orchard felt like the safest place in the world.


Cyrene then leaned back against the low orchard fence, arms crossed loosely as she tilted her head toward Phainon. 


“So…” she began, a playful note in her voice. “What’s he like? The King of Kremnos. In person.”


Phainon snorted, picking a stray leaf from his sleeve. “Mydeimos?”


“Mhm.”


He huffed, rubbing his face as though trying to scrub the man out of his memory. “He’s… impossible.”


Cyrene’s lips curled. "Awful?”


“Oh no, not that bad.” Phainon waved a hand vaguely at the sky. “Just, impossibly smug. Arrogant. Showy. Always walking around half-naked like he’s some sort of divine statue come to life. And don’t get me started on how he drinks like he’s starring in an erotic play every time he lifts a goblet.”


Cyrene faked a gasp. “So you were looking at him indecently.”


“I...!” Phainon’s mouth opened. Closed. Opened again. “That’s not the point.”


Cyrene laughed.


Phainon groaned, rubbing at his temple. “He's strong, fine, ridiculously strong. Barehanded, even. Fights like a beast. And when he smiles, which is rare, he looks like he’s about to either kiss you or kill you. Sometimes both.”


"You, kissed him?"


"NO!!!"


“Haha, he sounds so intense though,” she said, smirking.


“He is,” Phainon admitted. “And somehow calm. And smart. I heard he loves reading too. His office’s full of papers. Wears these stupid glasses too.”


“Glasses?”


Phainon threw his hands up, then mimicking the said accessory with his fingers. “And they make him look even better! Like a sensible tyrant. I can’t explain it.”


Cyrene’s laughter broke through the quiet trees. “You sound like you like him quite a lot.”


“What?!” Phainon practically flailed upright, cheeks flushing. “No! I’m just explaining how...uh, how ridiculous he is. I mean, come on. He’s not even my type!”


“Sure.”


“I mean it! My type is someone soft. Gentle. Smaller than me. A little wild, maybe, but shy. Like a cat.”


Cyrene blinked. “A… cat.”


Phainon nodded solemnly. “A very specific cat I told you about. My cutie kitty. That’s the one I’m holding out for.”


She raised an eyebrow, entirely unconvinced.


“Mydeimos is nothing like that,” he continued defiantly. “He’s all showy, brute force and dangerous stares. He has no shame and walk around with his chest exposed. Not my taste. At all.”


“Absolutely. You're not intersted in him, not at all,” Cyrene echoed with mock sincerity.


Phainon squinted at her, then grinned and looped his arm around her shoulders. “Alright, alright, that’s enough teasing.” He ruffled her hair with exaggerated carelessness. “You’re lucky I’m feeling nice today.”


“Ugh, stop, Phainon!” She tried to duck, laughing as she shoved at his arm. “You’re messing my hair!”


The orchard rustled softly with the passing breeze, sweet with the scent of ripened fruit and summer soil. Cyrene’s laughter still lingered faintly in the air when a new voice, low and smooth like still water, slipped into their conversation.


“I didn’t expect a welcome, given I came unannounced,” the man said. “But I certainly didn’t expect to find my own queen in the middle of an affair.”


Phainon nearly jumped out of his skin.


He whipped around so fast he tripped over his own foot and caught himself on the fence, eyes widening at the figure standing just beyond the trees.


Mydeimos.


He looked nothing like the golden warlord who stood bloodied yet remained beautiful. Gone was the gleaming armor and bare chest. In its place: a soft earth-brown tunic cinched with a travel-worn belt, black trousers tucked into sturdy boots, and a dusky green cloak falling in quiet folds over his shoulders. A hood hung loose behind his neck. He bore no insignia, no royal emblem, just a man. And yet, he looked no less charming.


More than that, his voice was calm. Carefully so. Too calm. Every syllable measured and smooth, the way a knife might whisper against whetstone.


Phainon’s skin prickled.


“It’s not an affair,” he stammered, eyes darting to Cyrene like a lifeline. “This is Cyrene. She’s like a sister to me!”


Cyrene bowed politely, her posture impeccable despite the rising tension. “Your Majesty.”


Mydeimos gave her the barest nod, but his gaze never left Phainon. He didn’t even blink.


Phainon cleared his throat, adjusting his shirt like it might shield him from the weight of that stare. “What are you doing here? Shouldn’t you be... busy? You know, doing kingly paperwork, intimidating nobles, drinking weird wine on your throne?”


"Is that how you think of my life as ruler?" Mydeimos tilted his head slightly. “Anyway, I’m here to see my queen.”


“Wait," Phainon's eyes widened just slightly. "The three days aren’t even over yet!”


A sigh escaped Mydeimos, exasperatedly. “We are spouses, are we not? It’s only natural I greet your parents. Formally.”


Phainon opened his mouth. Then closed it. Then opened it again.


“You, wait, what?! You came here to meet my parents?!”


But Mydeimos was already walking as if bored by Phainon's endless question. His boots crunched lightly against the earth as he strode down the orchard path, eyes scanning the rows of humble homes ahead.


“Which one is your house?”


Phainon gawked, half in disbelief. “O, oi, wait!” he called, stumbling after him. “You can’t just...! I mean, hey! Could you slow down?!”


He looked back once at Cyrene, who stood wide-eyed under the shade of the trees, blinking rapidly like someone who had just seen a deer sprout wings.


Phainon mouthed a hurried “I’m sorry” before he rushed after the king of Kremnos, who was apparently hellbent on meeting his future in-laws in his forest-camouflage outfit like this was all perfectly normal.


Cyrene, left in the orchard with the echo of soft footfalls fading into the summer breeze, slowly broke into a grin.


“Well,” she murmured, shaking her head with an incredulous smile. “Maybe I don’t have to worry about him after all.”

**
