chapters.html:
The path narrowed as they walked shoulder to shoulder, the gravel crunching underfoot. Sunlight filtered through the canopy of grapevines stretched across wooden trellises, casting soft mottled shadows over their steps.


Phainon broke the silence first, eyeing the traveler’s cloak draped over Mydeimos’ frame. “So… what’s with the outfit?” he asked, half teasing. “You look like you're trying to smuggle potatoes instead of being, you know, a king.”


Mydeimos didn’t look at him, but the corner of his mouth twitched slightly. “Would you prefer I came dressed as always?”


Phainon flushed. “Wha, No!” he blurted, cracking in the middle. “Absolutely not! I mean, you can’t just...naked? In front of my parents?!”


“I didn’t say I'd come naked in front of your parents,” Mydeimos replied smoothly, still not meeting his gaze.


Phainon sputtered. His ears burned so brightly he was sure a passing bee might mistake them for tulips.


Mydeimos glanced sidelong at him, golden eyes were always seemed so hard to decipher. “I dressed plainly to avoid attention. I doubt people here would be happy to see Kremnoan King visited without warning.”


That last word came quiet. Almost uncharacteristically gentle.


Phainon blinked, caught off guard.


“So that’s why you didn’t come with me and decided to come alone?” he asked. “Didn’t want the royal fanfare?”


Mydeimos kept walking. “I figured maybe you need time with your family.”


The answer was curt, but something in it felt too gentle. Phainon didn’t push. He just turned his gaze ahead, toward the slowly appearing outline of his home beyond the barley fields.


Still, he caught the way Mydeimos’ eyes wandered as they passed the heart of the village, small stone cottages with flowering windowsills, lines of laundry dancing in the wind, children running barefoot and shrieking with laughter, goats sunbathing like tiny, smug nobles.


“It’s not much in this small town. A capital, they said but this place is smaller than your whole palace,” Phainon said with a grin, “but I’m proud of my hometown, though.”


Mydeimos didn’t reply immediately, but his gaze lingered a touch longer on a child being scolded gently by a grandmother with flour-dusted hands.


“I can see that,” he finally said, quieter than before.


Emboldened, Phainon grinned and took a sharp left turn, nudging Mydeimos with his elbow. “Come on, I'll give you a short tour. That’s the baker’s house, he makes the worst bread in the world, but his daughter plays the lyre like a goddess. And over there, that’s where I used to sneak in during harvest season just to steal peaches.”


“You stole?” Mydeimos arched an eyebrow.


Phainon puffed his chest. “Borrowed permanently. Aedes Elysiae's customs.”


As they passed, villagers slowed, eyes following them. Some paused mid-step, others mid-chore. A few recognized Phainon immediately, waving or calling out warm greetings.


“There’s our hero!”


“Welcome back, Phai!”


“You’re alive! Thank the gods!”


Phainon laughed, raising a hand to wave at them. “Yeah, yeah, I’m back! Still in one piece!”


More eyes turned curiously to Mydeimos, who remained mostly silent behind Phainon’s broad frame. A few people whispered, eyebrows raised.


“Who’s that with him?”


“Looks like a traveler…”


Phainon leaned slightly toward Mydeimos, whispering sideways out of the corner of his mouth. “Just act normal. Smile, maybe. Or don’t. Smiling might terrify them more.”


“I’m not here to win popularity,” Mydeimos muttered.


“No kidding,” Phainon murmured under his breath, though the fondness in his voice softened the jab.


He waved at a couple more curious onlookers and gave a sheepish, half-hearted “just a friend visiting” excuse to a nosy uncle before steering them away from the busier alley.


It was strange, he thought, glancing at the stoic man beside him. The same Mydeimos who fought him for ten days and ten nights, who held his fate on a blade’s edge, now walking past the farm he grew up tending, his head slightly turned toward the rows of wildflowers blooming between fence posts.


Phainon swallowed the odd flutter in his chest.


If anyone had told him two months ago that he’d be parading his newlywed tyrant husband through the hometown's mundane routine in disguise, Phainon would've told them to lay off the fermented goat’s milk.


But fate always worked in strange twist.


The sun had dipped lower now, casting a honeyed glow across the wheat fields and painting their house in gold and rose. Phainon led Mydeimos through the narrow path between the vegetable beds, up to the weathered wooden steps of his home.


His father, Hieronymus, was in the front yard splitting wood, his sleeves rolled up, rhythm steady and practiced. A rough thud of axe meeting log punctuated the birdsong.


His mother, Audata, stood by the edge of the porch, watering the row of clay pots brimming with mint and feverfew. Her back was straight, eyes focused on the gentle motion of her watering can until her gaze lifted and she lit up.


“Phainon!” she called, joy in her voice. “Welcome home, darling! Oh, I thought you'd stay out longer!”


She set the can down and wiped her hands on her apron, starting toward him with open arms, only to falter mid-step.


Her eyes landed on the tall man trailing a step behind Phainon.


The stranger.


She blinked, once, twice. Her smile dimmed. Her brows knitted together.


“Who is this?” she asked, the warmth vanished and her eyes narrowing faintly. “A friend of yours?”


Phainon’s mouth opened, then closed again. “Uh, well...he's—”


But before he could sputter an answer, Mydeimos stepped forward.


He placed a hand over his chest and bowed his head with quiet dignity. “I am Mydeimos, King of Kremnos,” he said smoothly, respectful regardless his title. “And as you might've heard, I've married your son.”


A sharp inhale. A gasp. And then the sound of an axe slipping from stunned fingers and landing on the ground with a dull thud.


Hieronymus stared.


Audata’s eyes widened, color draining from her face. Her fingers gripped Phainon’s arm instinctively, pulling him ever so slightly back toward her side, shielding him like she used to when he was a boy.


There was silence. Tense. Cracked.


“I see...” she said softly, wary. “And what does the King of Kremnos want from my son now? I doubt our humble house has something precious to offer after you claimed our only son.”


Phainon winced. “Mom...”


Mydeimos, however, didn’t bristle. He didn’t seem surprised. His posture remained upright, respectful, even as his shoulders tensed ever so slightly under the cloak.


“I apologize if my presence is unwelcome,” he said gently. “It was not my intention to intrude.”


His gaze flickered to Hieronymus and Audata in turn.


“Regardless the situation, both of you are Phainon's cherished parents and I only wished to greet you in person as... a son-in-law, if I may be conceited to call myself as such. You raised a remarkable man.”


He smiled faintly. A soft, crooked smile, beautiful, but strange, like a glimpse through a window just before it shut again. There was something fractured in it. Something sincere, tinged with pang of agony.


Then he bowed deeply, unbecoming for a king and then turned away, leaving.


The silence that followed Mydeimos’ departure sat heavy in the air, like storm clouds that hadn’t decided whether to break or cease. Phainon stood there too long, eyes fixed on the path where his so-called-husband had walked away, the weight in his chest too complex to name.


Behind him, his father was the first to speak.


“…He wasn’t what I expected,” Hieronymus muttered, as if confessing to no one in particular.


Audata, still watching her son, slowly nodded. "Right..."


“I thought the King of Kremnos would speak like a blade to fear.” His father let out a low breath. “But he sounded more like a man who...” he paused, searching for the word, "had lost too many things.”


“Or was afraid of something,” Audata added quietly.


Phainon turned to them, mouth opening, guilt washing over his face like a tide. “Mom, I...”


But he didn’t finish.


He didn’t have to.


Audata smiled before he could form the words, gently brushing dust from his shoulder like she used to when he was little. “Go after him.”


Phainon batted his lashes, fast.


“Bring your husband back,” she repeated, softer now, eyes brimming with something unshed and knowing. “I made your favourite stew. He shouldn’t miss it.”


A second passed before Phainon’s face broke tenderly, touched by his mother's understanding. “Mom…”


“Tell him our house might not big but enough to host him, might as well stay for the night.”


He grinned and nodded. “Thank you.” Then he turned on his heels and sprinted off.


He didn’t know why he ran with such urgency. Maybe it was the way Mydeimos had bowed his head before turning. Or that flicker of pain in his smile. Or maybe it was something deeper, a pressure building in his chest that screamed: Don’t let him go. Not like this.


The dirt road stretched ahead, splitting into winding trails between houses and fields, and Mydeimos was nowhere to be seen.


Phainon stopped at the fork, chest heaving. “Damn it—”


He spun around, eyes scanning every path, every tree, even the rooftops. Where could he have gone so fast?


He ran again, down one path, calling out in his head even as his mouth stayed shut. His heart pounded against his ribs. Why he was so bothered? He wasn’t sure how, but he also knew that if he didn’t chase him now, he’d regret it forever.


Phainon ran, lungs burning and feet pounding against the earth, the village slowly thinning behind him. His hair stuck to his skin, sweat running down his back, but he didn’t stop.


He didn’t even know where his feet were leading him until the trees began to thin into a familiar clearing. The grass was taller now, the stones weathered with time, but the place still held the hush of childhood secrets.


And then he saw him.


There, perched on the broad flat stone near the edge of the shallow brook, sat Mydeimos. In a simple tunic, pants tucked into worn boots, cloak folded beside him, hair slightly mussed by wind.


Exactly like how Phainon remembered the boy from all those years ago.


His breath caught.


Without the heavy crown and titles, stripped of grandeur and pretense, there was no room for denial anymore. He saw the shadow of past merged with the present. The sloped eyes, those red-tinged markings, the solemn curve of his lips when he thought no one was watching.


He was the one that Phainon had been waiting for so long.


Maybe he hadn’t grown into the delicate beauty Phainon once imagined, maybe he had traded it for solid strength, broader shoulders, and storm-worn hands. But now, under the fading sun light, he didn't seem to change at all.


Still hurting in silence, still so lonely.


Phainon stood there, quiet for a long while, chest rising and falling. Then, with a voice that was soft and vulnerable, he said:


“…I waited.”


Mydeimos turned at the sound. His golden eyes met Phainon’s and for the first time, they looked fragile. Not cold or calculating, not amused or wary. Just helplessly vulnerable.


“I waited so long,” Phainon breathed again, stepping closer.


Mydeimos looked down at his own hands. “…I’m sorry.”


“For what?”


“For not becoming what you hoped for. For not being… someone your parents would welcome.”


Phainon slowly moved beside him and sat down, the stone cool against his thighs. For a moment, they just listened to the quiet ripple of water and the breeze weaving through tall grass.


“…Did you always know?” Phainon asked at last.


Mydeimos nodded faintly. “I didn't know the name of this place so I didn't think much when the delegates arrived. But when I saw you. That day in the throne room, in that ridiculous gown,” he gave a quiet huff of laughter, “I recognized you right away. You still had that same look in your eyes.”


Phainon blinked. “Why didn’t you say anything?”


“Well, because time passed.” Mydeimos admitted, gaze fell to somewhere distant. "I changed. Maybe you too."


Phainon was silent.


“That was why,” Mydeimos went on, “I tried to send you back home, maybe pardoning your hometown because this place had been nothing but kind to me. But, you just had to be stubborn and challenged me.”


“Right,” Phainon murmured. “…And you accepted.”


“How could I not? I’m a king. If I back down in my own colosseum, I lose everything.”


Phainon hummed in response, now everything clicked. Like how he was treated like a guest than prisoner after the fight, why the royal knights were so considerate for this town. Mydeimos must've get his hands around for Phainon's comfort.


“...Did you hold back?” Phainon asked suddenly, looking at him. “Be honest.”


Mydeimos blinked, then let out a scoff. “Hold back? No. That will be rude. Not many know because I'm always seen with my mother's spear but I'm actually a fistfighter. So yes, that was me, giving everything I had. Every punch. Every dodge. You were good.”


Phainon’s gaze lingered on Mydeimos’s hands. It looked flawless but he knew, he heard how many battles he went through. He remembered gripping them in the colosseum, remembered the way they struck and held with equal force. He remembered all the bloods he spilled from Mydeimos' undying body.


He swallowed thickly. “I’m sorry.”


Mydeimos turned to him, brows lifting slightly.


“For hurting you,” Phainon murmured. “I didn’t hold back either.”


A low chuckle escaped Mydeimos, surprisingly soft. “You did it to protect your home. Don’t apologize for that.” He glanced away. “I would be offended if you didn’t give your everything.”


Phainon let the words settle. A strange comfort bloomed in his chest, fragile but warm.


“When did you notice?”


Phainon blinked. “…Notice what?”


“That I was, you know, me.”

Phainon gave a rueful little laugh, rubbing the back of his neck. “Maybe… from the start. I don’t know. Something about you felt familiar. Your eyes, your voice. The way you looked at me sometimes, you feel too much like, well, you. And those red markings. I might be convinced if all Kremnoan had the similar marking but no, you're the only one...”

“And yet?” Mydeimos prompted, tilting his head.

Phainon sighed, lips twisting. “I told myself you couldn’t be him.”

Mydeimos smirked faintly. “Because I was ‘brute, violent, half-naked, and definitely not your type’?”

Phainon let out an audible groan and buried his face in his hands. “You heard that?”

“Every word,” Mydeimos said, deadpan.

Phainon peeked through his fingers, face flushed. “I was trying to convince myself, alright? It felt like betrayal. Like I was about to fall for someone who wasn’t him, my first crush, my kitten boy.”

“Mm,” Mydeimos leaned back on his hands. “It does sound like something a honest fool who kept a crush for years would think.”

“You’re not one to talk,” Phainon shot back. “You knew who I was, didn’t say anything, and still agreed to marry me.”

“That was survival,” Mydeimos quipped, then exhaled slowly. The humor faded, replaced with something heavier. “What you did was a crime. Against the throne. Against Kremnos. You knew that.”

Phainon’s throat tightened. “I know.”

“To uphold the rules, I could have had you imprisoned,” Mydeimos said quietly. “Or executed.”

“…So you married me instead.”

“I made a choice. One that would stabilize things, give us time.”

Phainon glanced sideways. “Time?”

“To figure it out,” Mydeimos said, calmly. “I’ll hold the marriage for a few years. Keep the political peace. Let your kingdom breathe.”

Phainon blinked at him.

“Then,” Mydeimos continued, “when the storm settles… I’ll divorce you. I'll find a good excuse for that without throwing fire to your land.”

The words landed heavier than either expected.

Phainon couldn’t speak for a moment. It wasn’t that he hadn’t imagined the possibility but hearing it aloud, so plainly stated, left a hollow echo in his chest.

“Then, you’ll go back to your family,” Mydeimos said, not looking at him. “Your farm. Your quiet town. They’ll welcome you.”

“…And what about you?”

“I’m the King of Kremnos,” Mydeimos answered with a thin smile adorned his visage. “I’ll survive.”

But his voice, for once, didn’t sound like stone or steel.

It sounded like something softer.

And lonelier.

Phainon huffed, arms crossing, lower lip jutting ever so slightly.

“You know,” he mumbled, eyes not meeting Mydeimos, “you keep deciding things by yourself.”

Mydeimos turned his head, puzzled. “What do you mean?”

Phainon’s voice grew sharper, petulant. “You came into my life uninvited. You stole my heart and vanished. Then you reappeared, not as that sweet boy I once knew, but as a half-naked menace everyone feared. You made me chose a duel, forced me into a marriage. Now you’re telling me we’ll get divorced in a few years like I’m just a piece on your board.”

His voice trembled, not from anger but from the sheer weight of unshed feelings. “When is it my turn to decide something?”

Mydeimos’s eyes widened, mouth slightly agape. He blinked once, then slowly furrowed his brows as if struggling to find the words.

“…Then what do you want to decide, Phainon?”

Phainon met his gaze and smiled.

Not the playful, smug curve of lips he used to tease and deflect.

But something quieter. Braver. A smile that knew sorrow and still chose to reach out.

“I want this,” he murmured.

Then, without warning, without flourish, he reached out, gently cupping Mydeimos’s cheek with his calloused hand, fingers curling just beneath the edge of that wind-kissed jaw. Mydeimos inhaled sharply, golden eyes widening as if no one had ever dared to touch him like that. Like he was precious. Like he was soft.

Their faces were close now, too close.

Phainon’s voice was only a breath away from being silenced. "Can I?”

Mydeimos knew the implication and didn't pull away. That was enough. Phainon whispered a gratitude and leaned in, gently overlapping their lips.

No fire. No frenzy.

Only warmth, tender and vulnerable. The kiss didn’t demand or claim. It offered. Like an outstretched hand on a cold morning.

Mydeimos gasped faintly into it. Phainon felt it: that sudden shiver, the way his body tensed in surprise… and then eased. Mydeimos’s lashes fluttered shut, and he leaned forward as if he didn’t trust himself to let go. His hand came up, not to push away, but to hold Phainon's waist, grounding himself in that moment.

Their lips moved slowly. Uncertainly. Like they were relearning a language they’d once spoken fluently as children.

It was soft. Sincere.

And when they pulled apart, foreheads brushing, breaths tangled in the silence, it wasn’t desire that lingered, but ache. A shared ache, stretched across years and kingdoms.

Phainon chuckled weakly. “That’s what I want to decide, dear husband.”

Mydeimos was silent, his expression unreadable at first. His lips, kissed and parted, trembled just slightly. Then he let out a breath through his nose, somewhere between a sigh and a laugh.

“You’re a reckless idiot,” he muttered.

Phainon grinned. “Too late for that, you already married to me.”

“…I guess so.”

And in that soft glow of a fading afternoon, where shadows stretched and cicadas hummed low in the trees, Mydeimos' hand rested on Phainon’s, and they held on each other, reassuringly.

“We’ve got a lot to talk about, you and I,” Phainon's grin stretched out. “But first, we need to go home. My mother said we're having feast.”

Mydeimos paused, golden eyes shifting toward the horizon, toward the little house nestled by the field. There was hesitation in the set of his shoulders, in the way he shifted his weight like someone preparing to retreat. But Phainon just held out his hand, open, steady, insistent.

It felt so familiar. That gesture. It almost mimicking their shared childhood, where Phainon would always drag Mydeimos around for fun.

And maybe that was why Mydeimos hesitated, he might destroy the fond memory. But before he could refuse, Phainon cackled and grabbed his hand anyway, strong fingers wrapping around his palm.

“It’ll be fine,” he said, laughing as he yanked Mydeimos forward. “Just run with me.”

Across the golden field that shimmered under the late afternoon sun, through the narrow, winding road that led past the village well and stone plaza. Mydeimos’ hair looked wild in the wind, and Phainon never let go. For a few fleeting seconds, it felt like they were those boys again, one wild and grinning, the other trailing behind but never too far. No titles. No crowns. Just two hands locked through the years.

They burst into the yard breathless, laughing like fools. Mydeimos stopped at the edge, catching his breath. He didn't move, still unsure. Phainon turned, face flushed from the run, but his eyes were still annoyingly bright. Without a word, he reached for Mydeimos again and laced their fingers.

“I told you it’ll be okay,” he whispered, squeezing.

Then together, they stepped into the house.

Inside, Audata and Hieronymus were already standing. The wooden table was set, the stew simmering in the hearth. The smell of seasoned roast and fresh-baked bread lingered in the air but tension curled like smoke between the walls.

Both parents stood stiffly as the door creaked shut behind them. Their gazes went straight to Mydeimos.

He looked down briefly, as if instinctively expecting a blow. “Phainon, I'll just wait outside."

“No,” Phainon said, loud enough to cut through the unease. He tightened his grip on Mydeimos’s hand, stepping forward with conviction.

“Mother, Father,” he said, meeting their eyes. “This is Mydeimos. He's the man I chose to marry.”

The room went quiet. His parents exchanged a look. For a heartbeat, no one spoke.

Then Hieronymus cleared his throat. “Well,” he said, a little awkward, “welcome home.”

Audata stepped forward next. Her eyes were still searching, still cautious, but gentler. “Come in, Mydeimos,” she said at last. “I hope you like stew. It's Phainon's favourite.”

Mydeimos batted his eyelashes, fast. Something shifted behind his eyes, surprise, maybe even a flicker of uncertainty. Phainon noticed how his usually sharp shoulders lowered just slightly.

"Come, let's eat! I'm starving."

They all moved to the table. Mydeimos sat carefully on the cushion offered, looking more awkward than Phainon had ever seen him. He glanced at the utensils like they might bite, unsure of what to do with the little folded napkin Audata placed by his hand.

“You don’t have to look like someone led to execution,” Phainon murmured under his breath, nudging him with his elbow. “It’s just dinner.”

Mydeimos shot him a sharp look, but it had no bite, only a faint flush creeping up his neck.

To anyone else, he was the infamous immortal king, untouchable and cold.

But in this little house, with the scent of herbs and soft firelight dancing in the hearth, he looked like a man trying to remember what peace tasted like.

Alas, dinner began with tension so thick, it could’ve been carved like the roast on the table.

Mydeimos still sat with straight-backed posture and hands clasped too neatly on his lap, his usual armor of indifference traded for something far more brittle, uncertainty. He barely touched the stew at first, eyes darting from Audata’s gentle smile to Hieronymus’s quiet scrutiny like he was awaiting some unspoken judgment.

Phainon didn’t say much either just quietly watching, letting his foot occasionally bump against Mydeimos’ like a quiet reminder: You’re not alone.

But then Audata, sharp as ever, noticed how little Mydeimos had eaten and, with the tone only a mother could wield, pointed her spoon at him. “You’re eating too small for a man in my family,” she said. “Eat more.”

Mydeimos blinked, as if stunned by the declaration. “I, I’ve eaten enough.”

“Rubbish. You call that enough?" She added more portion onto Mydeimos' bowl, made the blond widened his eyes. "Eat, or you'll stand in the corner.”

"I, I understand." And he did.

From there, things softened. Somehow the awkward air began to thaw. Audata ladled more and more soup into his bowl. Hieronymus offered him slices of honey-roasted root vegetables, and when Mydeimos hesitated, the old man nudged the plate closer like a silent challenge.

They spoke of the field, of the weather, of the coming harvest and how Phainon once broke a rake because he insisted it doubled as a sword. Mydeimos didn’t speak much. Mostly nodded, listening, but there was a rare flicker of amusement in his eyes. Even when Phainon rolled his eyes and said, “You’re telling all my childhood crimes,” Mydeimos had a tender smile on his visage.

And when dinner ended and they stepped out into the cool evening air, Mydeimos looked almost dazed. He didn’t say it, but Phainon could see it in the way he kept glancing back at the door like he couldn’t believe any of it was real.

“Come,” Phainon said, bumping their shoulders as he led him down the familiar cobbled path. “Let’s walk.”

They didn’t go far. Just a slow meander through the lamplit village, past the plaza, the shuttered stalls and quiet homes. Children’s laughter echoed faintly in the distance, the scent of burning wood clung to the breeze.

“You were so quiet back there,” Phainon said.

“I didn’t want to scare them.”

Phainon chuckled. “You just got bullied into eating three bowls of stew and a full plate of vegetables.”

Mydeimos gave him a withering look. “I was being polite.”

“You looked like you wanted to run and hide.”

A short silence. Then Mydeimos muttered, “...Your mother is scary.”

Phainon snorted.

They teased, traded old stories and jabs, occasionally bumping shoulders as they walked back under the stars. The village felt smaller in the dark, but in a comforting way. It felt like they’d carved out a little pocket of time, just for them.

When they returned to Phainon’s house and quietly stepped into his room, they both froze.

Two beds.

Two small, neatly made beds side by side on the wooden floor, warm blankets folded and pillows fluffed. Clearly set up by Phainon’s parents with acceptance that their only son was now married.

A heavy silence fell over them.

“…I’ll sleep outside,” Mydeimos said, already half-turning back toward the door.

Phainon grabbed his wrist. “What? Why?”

“You might be uncomfortable.” Mydeimos avoided his gaze.

“Do you not want to sleep with me that much?” Phainon asked flatly, squinting. “You can just say so. I can take it.”

Mydeimos blinked, then frowned. “That’s not it.”

Phainon crossed his arms. “Then what? I’ve shared beds with drunk nobles, runaway goats. Sleeping next to you is probably the least dangerous thing I’ve ever done.”

“…Goats?”

“Don’t ask.”

Mydeimos sighed, rubbing his temple.

“So?” Phainon raised a brow. “Are you staying or do I have to chain you to the leg of the bed?”

A scowl flickered across Mydeimos’s face, but it didn’t quite reach his eyes. He finally stepped back into the room and muttered, “Fine. Just don’t snore”

Phainon grinned as he pulled the door shut. “No promises.”

And that night, the two of them settled into the little beds side by side, the silence between them but it was no longer heavy. No longer cold. Just a quiet space shared between two bodies who had wandered far and finally, finally began to drift home.

The morning mist still clung to the village when Mydeimos stirred.

Phainon, on the other hand, slept like the world could end and he wouldn't notice. Mouth wide open, one leg flung off the bed, a trail of drool glistening at the corner of his lips. His hair was a tangle of soft blue waves against the pillow, chest rising and falling in slow rhythm. Mydeimos sat up quietly, squinting at the utterly undignified scene next to him.

“…How charming,” he murmured, softly chuckled.

He rose without a sound and pulled the blanket higher over Phainon's shoulder, pausing just briefly to take in the curve of his back, the warmth in his face even in sleep. Then he stepped away and slipped quietly out the door.

Outside, the sky was still pale with dawn. The faint scent of dew-covered soil mingled with the sharp bite of chopped wood.

There, just a few paces from the house, Hieronymus stood in the yard with sleeves rolled up, splitting firewood with practiced swings of the axe. The rhythmic thunk of blade meeting bark echoed through the quiet.

Mydeimos approached with measured steps and offered a respectful nod. “Good morning.”

Hieronymus straightened a little, wiping the sweat from his brow with the back of his hand. “Morning,” he replied, short but not unfriendly.

Mydeimos’s eyes drifted to the log pile, then to the axe in Hieronymus's grip. “May I?”

The older man blinked, surprised. “You sure?”

Mydeimos only nodded.

Hieronymus studied him for a moment longer, then silently offered the axe. Mydeimos stepped forward, rolled his shoulders once, and brought it down in a clean, effortless motion. The wood split perfectly.

“...Not bad,” Hieronymus muttered.

“I’ve done this before,” Mydeimos said calmly. Another swing, another clean cut.

“You?” the man asked, brow raised. “Seems a strange skill for a king.”

Mydeimos gave a quiet chuckle, the kind that barely lifted his shoulders. “I wasn’t born one. For some years… I had no roof over my head. This kind of work kept me warm.”

The axe thudded again, and the pieces of firewood tumbled apart neatly.

Silence passed between them, not uncomfortable, just heavy with the things not said.

Then, the door creaked open.

Audata stepped out into the soft gold of morning, a cloth draped over one arm and a steaming kettle in her hand. She squinted toward them, then called, “That’s enough for now. You’ll ruin your backs before midday.”

"Alright." Hieronymus said, stretched his arms.

Meanwhile, Mydeimos paused mid-swing, straightening. He wasn't sure if he should stop or not.

But then, Audata called out again, but her voice came gentler this time.

“Mydeimos, here's your tea. There's pound cake too.”

Mydeimos glanced toward Hieronymus, who simply patting him twice on the shoulder and followed his wife to the porch.

With a breath drawn into his chest, Mydeimos left the axe embedded in the stump and walked to join them.

He sat on the wooden steps as Audata poured the tea, its aroma fragrant with herbs and a hint of honey. She handed him a cup, warm in his hand, and then one to her husband.

They didn’t speak for a while. Just sipped quietly, watching the sunlight spread slowly over the village rooftops. Birds chirped in the hedges. Somewhere, a child’s laughter echoed faintly.

It was nothing like the grand palace halls or war-bathed colosseums.

But to Mydeimos, this quiet moment, this porch, this tea, felt heavier than any crown he had ever worn.

And warmer than he expected.

The tranquility stretched, the three sat side by side, warmed by sun and entertained by chirping birds.

Then, gently, Audata broke the silence.

“…I apologise,” she said softly although still with a ragged edge. “For how I treated you yesterday.”

Mydeimos turned slightly, eyes widening just a little.

“There’s no need,” he said, his voice dropped low, quiet as the wind brushing through the flower pots nearby. “Your reaction was… expected. I wouldn’t welcome someone like me either." He spelt it with a smile.

But that smile made something ache in Audata’s chest.

She looked away for a moment, unable to meet those golden eyes that somehow looked older than they should.

“Then… why?” she asked, almost accusing. “Why not just return Phainon? Why keep him in Kremnos? What is it that you want from him?”

“Dear...” Hieronymus shook his head, stopping her, but Mydeimos didn’t flinch.

He just… smiled again. Smaller this time. Sadder.

“I want nothing,” he said. “Nothing but his safety. I want to protect him.”

The words lingered in the air, steady as stone. “If I could,” Mydeimos went on, “I would return him to this home. To your warmth. To the people he loves. But...”

He paused, fingers tightening just slightly on the tea cup.

“But the truth is, he trespassed into Kremnos under a false identity. And fought me in the colosseum. That… is not something that can be forgiven easily by my court.”

He looked down. “I am king, but I am not omnipotent. There are laws, blood-soaked and old, and those laws would have demanded his execution. Marriage… was the only way I could shield him.” A bitter smile curled at the edge of his lips. “Forgive me, for being so powerless.”

Audata stared at him. She studied his visage, reading more than his words could ever tell. Then, without a word, she shifted, reaching across the small distance between them. Her hand hovered, trembled slightly, but then it settled gently on his cheek. Her thumb brushed the marking just beneath his eye.

“You saved my son,” she whispered. “He came home alive. That is more than I ever dared hope.”

Mydeimos didn’t speak. He simply closed his eyes for a moment, leaning into her touch.

And in a voice gentler than the wind, he said, “I swear I’ll protect him. With everything I have. So… please. Trust me.”

A long silence followed.

Then, from beside them, Hieronymus gave a huff. “Well. You’ve got a task ahead of you then.”

Mydeimos blinked, surprised.

The older man crossed his arms, eyeing him with a resigned look. “Phainon is reckless and so stubborn. He’s like his mother that way. Once he’s made up his mind, no one’s going to make him budge, not even us.”

Audata scowled but didn’t disagree.

A faint smile pulled at Mydeimos’s lips. “Yes. I’ve noticed.”

“He clearly fancies you,” Hieronymus said with a rough sigh of fatherly exasperation. "And exactly because of that, he'll likely create more trouble than you thought you signed for."

"I am well prepared for that."

“Haha, I'm sure you are. Just… let him come visit us every now and then,” Hieronymus added. “Or better, come with him. We’ve got more room than it looks. And I suppose you can help split the wood again. Maybe we'll grow crops together? Or is that too much for a king?”

Mydeimos looked surprised for a moment.

Then he shook his head. “It might be not for a king but I'm Phainon's spouse. So no, it's not too much,” he said. “And if you ever wish to visit Kremnos, simply send word. The gates will always open for you.”

Audata’s eyes shimmered, but this time, her smile was real.

Their son’s husband was not what they expected but neither was their son’s courage. Perhaps this was how fate unfolded: not clean, not easy… But they willingly to slowly learning how to trust the man than the rumours about him.

The day passed like a gentle stream, sunlight pouring through the fields and dappling the earth with gold. Phainon had expected Mydeimos to stiffen, maybe complain, when he offered to show him the ropes of farm life but to his shock, Mydeimos picked up the hoe like he’d done it all his life.

Mydeimos straightened, brushing dirt from his hands. “If I were truly a tyrant, I would’ve had you executed the moment you pulled off that gown and challenged me.”

Mydeimos gave him a look. "You looked ridiculous in it."

Mydeimos didn’t miss a beat. “And you did end up as a bride.”

Mydeimos didn’t answer that, he just smirked, walking past him with the hoe slung over his shoulder.

“What?” Phainon asked.

Mydeimos looked away. “Your hair’s covered in hay.”

Another warm night passed and now Phainon’s parents stood on the porch, side by side, their eyes already red-rimmed though neither of them had shed a tear just yet. The sky was barely golden when the carriage bearing the Kremnoan sigil arrived, discreet and quiet, waiting beyond the field.

Phainon blinked, caught off guard. “Just… the usual. That he was ruthless. Tyrant. The kind of story parents tell their kids to make them behave.”

So he repeatedly told himself he was fine.


But when they got back to Kremnos, Mydeimos was everywhere except near him.


Apparently, a two-day absence was equivalent to a bureaucratic apocalypse. Mydeimos had returned to a mountain of documents, foreign letters, and reports from every stretch of the empire. And instead of pacing himself like a normal human, he threw himself headfirst into the work like he had something to prove.


The first week, Phainon let it slide. He even dropped by the war room just to lean over his husband's shoulder dramatically and whisper, “Don’t forget your loving queen awaits,” before being promptly kicked out by Krateros for bothering the king.


The second week, Mydeimos came to check in, a quick kiss pressed to his forehead and a muttered, “You’re not causing trouble, right?” before running off to deal with a mining revolt in the west.


By the fifth week, Phainon was beginning to feel less like a queen and more like an expensive houseplant.


It didn’t help that the palace was huge. A sprawling masterpiece of obsidian halls and gilded columns, full of rooms with names he couldn’t remember and doors that led to gardens, baths, libraries, even a mountain of treasures.


He had everything. Anything he wanted. All the attendants bowed. All the maids smiled. The cooks would whip up everything that Phainon couldn't even pronounce correctly.


But it wasn’t fun without Mydeimos.


He’d wander aimlessly with a bored expression and a well-dressed bodyguard trailing him like a shadow. He’d collapse on a silk lounge somewhere, stare at a chandelier, and dramatically mutter, “Bring me the king or drag the star down the sky for me.”


The guard never knew how to respond to that.


By the end of second month, Phainon found himself in the royal courtyard, chucking pieces of bread to fish pond just to watch them ripple.


He sighed.


Since when had he become like this? Clingy. Restless. Dreaming about someone else’s face more than he cared about his own reflection.


He poked the fish with a stick.


“I used to be cool,” he grumbled.


The fish blinked at him in what he interpreted as judgment.


“I did. I was a fearless warrior bride with broken sword, remember? Now look at me. Throwing grain at fish.”


He slumped back on the grass with a dramatic groan.


He missed him.


And he didn’t know how to say that without sounding like a lovesick idiot.


"Mydeimos, you jerk."


The sting of antiseptic made Phainon hiss between his teeth.


"Ow—ow ow ow, Hyacine, be gentle! That’s my favorite rib!"


"Then don’t go handing it like you have spare ribs in your wardrobe." Hyacine chirped with a grin, dabbing at his side. She had a smile even when she was scolding, which made it harder for Phainon to take her seriously… until the sting hit again. “You should stop asking people to spar with you if you wanted to stay pretty, Your Majesty.”


“I am pretty,” Phainon groaned dramatically. “Now I’m battle-scarred and pretty. That’s extra points.”


Hyacine wasn’t a native Kremnoan. She came from some distant place in the east. Her kind nature dancing around the Kremnoan's violence like it refused to be tamed. She’d only ended up in the castle because Mydeimos had seen her work at the border and told her, in his usual deadpan manner, “Kremnos needs a healer who doesn’t murder the patient.”


Across the infirmary, Castorice quietly chuckled. The older woman sat with legs neatly crossed, her hands wrapped around a teacup. Her lavender braid draped over one shoulder and her expression was as serene as ever. She was also non-native, brought to the castle for her knowledge.


On the other side were Dan Heng and Caelus, also non-Kremonan. Dan Heng was recruited for his ability to compile informations and arranging the documents chronologically. Meanwhile Caelus was being mysterious when asked why he lived in the castle.


Nonethless, apparently, Mydeimos had a hobby of adopting people he found useful. Phainon sometimes joked the castle was actually a glorified stray shelter.


The antiseptic stung again. Phainon hissed.


“Stay strong, Your Majesty,” Castorice said gently. “Kremnoan knights may not understand moderation, but they respect a challenge. You gave them one.”


Phainon let out a theatrical sigh and slumped on the cot. “Yeah, and now I’m paying the price.”


Hyacine dabbed another salve against a particularly nasty scrape on his shoulder. “What’s gotten into you, anyway? You’ve been mopey since His Majesty King left again.”


“I’m not mopey.”


“You’re fighting dozens of knights for fun." Caelus chirped. "If it was not sulking, then you're turning masochist."


Phainon went quiet. His eyes drifted to the window again, toward the sunlit garden, where the birds chirped without care. It all felt dull.


“I just…” he muttered. “Have either of you ever heard if Mydeimos… y’know, had someone before me?”


That made Hyacine pause mid-dab. She blinked. “What, like an ex?”


Castorice lowered her cup slightly. Her brows didn’t furrow, but her eyes widened slightly. The young men were exchanging look now.


“I’ve never heard such a thing,” Castorice said in her usual soft, melodic tone. “And I would know. I’ve served him long before any of you arrived.”


“Same,” Dan Heng added quickly. “Not even a record nor cheap gossip hinted it.”


Phainon exhaled like something deflated in his chest. “…Right.”


“Why are you asking?” Castorice asked gently.


Phainon shifted. “No reason. Just… curiosity.”


“Liar,” Hyacine said, poking his arm with the back of a salve brush. “You're jealous.”


“I’m not!”


“Ooh, you totally are!” Caelus teased. “Is this about the same thing? You asked if he was experienced and he said yes, and now you’re spiraling.”


Castorice’s eyes softened. “Ah. I see.”


Phainon groaned and flopped back. “I’m trying not to think about it.”


“But you are,” Dan Heng said, deadpanned.


Caelus cackled. “Bet you're still thinking of a mysterious lover from his past who, what, taught him how to be good with his mouth?”


Hyacine gasped, getting secondhand embarrassment. Dan Heng facepalmed.


"Caelus, don't be so vulgar about our king." Castorice reminded him but the gray-haired youth shrugged nonchalantly.


"Phainon's words, not mine, Cas."


Castorice then stood and walked closer, her steps silent. She reached out, placing a cold, light hand on Phainon’s bandaged one.


"We don't know much about his life before being our king. However, I believe His Majesty cherished you a lot."


Phainon stared at her. “I know...”


"But..?" Caelus asked, like knowing there was a continuity to that.


“…Do you think he’s cheating on me?”


The words slipped out before he could catch them.


And his friends were in sync, sprouting "What?" like Phainon just lost his mind.


Phainon sighed, shut his eyes.


“I don’t know,” he said, softly. “He’s been busy, and it’s fine, I get it, he’s the king and all. But he’s been gone for days. Doesn’t write. Doesn’t send anyone. And I know he cares, I do, but sometimes I just wonder. Maybe there’s someone he prefer than me so...” He broke off, pressing his fingers to his eyes. “Forget it. It’s stupid.”


Hyacine finally moved again, this time gentler. Her voice dropped to something quieter.


“You’re not stupid,” she said. 


"He is, though." Caelus quickly interjected but Hyacine hissed before she continued.

“But I don’t think you understand how you look when you’re near him.”


Phainon blinked. “How did I look?"


Hyacine beamed. “You light up like a bonfire. And so does he.”


Castorice nodded. “He may not show it like you do, but it’s there. He doesn’t waste time on things he doesn’t care about, you know.”


Phainon stayed quiet.


Caelus went closer, gave Phainon a light punch to his arm. “Our king might not be the kindest person in the world, but he is definitely not a cheater.”


"I agree," Dan Heng nodded solemnly, "he’s too possessive to want anyone else.”


Phainon let out a breath he didn’t know he was holding.


"Right. Sorry, guys." Phainon grinned. "I guess I got brain damage from those sparring, haha!"


Still, some part of him, soft and uncertain, twisted with ache.


He didn’t want to doubt.


But it was so easy to miss Mydei. Even more so to fear losing him.


Night had already fallen over Kremnos when Phainon was summoned to the study room.


He leapt from his seat because that meant Mydeimos had returned.


He’d lost track of how long his husband had been away. Five days? Six? Kremnos was always on fire in some part of its borders, and Mydeimos, of course, was always the one carrying the bucket of water. Still, this time, it had felt longer. And Phainon, for all his pride and sparkle, missed him.


That explained the stupid amount of time he spent soaking in the bath. And why he’d chosen his better tunic, brushed his hair thrice, and put on the perfume Hyacine said made him 'smell expensive'.


He was ready to pout, to complain, to demand attention with his usual sunshine dramatics and half-serious teasing. He had been waiting.


But as he pushed open the carved wooden doors and stepped into Mydeimos’ private study, every ounce of warm excitement drained from his face.


There was someone else there.


A young woman, maybe around his age. Not just standing beside Mydeimos but leaning over him. One arm braced against the back of his chair, the other loosely draped on Mydeimos' shoulder as if she owned the space between them. Her grayish hair was pinned up in a half-twist that let strands fall down her back. She was murmuring something while the two of them read from the same scroll, shoulders close enough that Phainon could’ve mistaken them for lovers in another context.


Phainon didn’t move. His smile, mid-forming, cracked and collapsed. He stood in the doorway like an intruder who walked into the wrong house. His breath caught halfway up his throat.


The girl noticed him first. Her eyes flicked up, sharp as aquamarine shards. She didn’t move away from Mydeimos. She just smiled, cat-like, almost mischievous.


"Well, hello. You must be the queen.” And there was zero respect, something that Phainon didn't expect from someone who he didn't even recognised.


Mydeimos didn’t even glance up. “You’re here. Sit down. We'll be done soon.”


His voice held no warmth, but that wasn’t new. Mydeimos was always composed like frost in spring. Still, Phainon obeyed, stiff-legged, and dropped onto the far couch like it was the only safe place not drenched in betrayal.


He tried not to scowl. He tried not to glare. He definitely tried not to notice that the girl had just touched his shoulder again.


Touched him. As if it were normal.


And Mydeimos didn’t even glance his way.


Phainon's stomach twisted, dark and hollow. Something acidic pooled under his ribs.


Cifera. That’s what Mydeimos called her.


Pretty name for a woman whose hands didn’t belong anywhere near his husband.


They were talking about policy. About a rebellion near the southern cliffs, something about the semantics in a treaty and some seamstress wished a meeting. None of it mattered. All Phainon could hear was Cifera’s airy laugh every time she teased Mydeimos. All he could see was how Mydeimos let her stay there, hovering, brushing his sleeve like she belonged in that space.


( Why is she that close to him? )


( Why is he letting her? )


Phainon’s fingers dug into his knees. He hated her. Irrationally. Fiercely. In a childish, biting, possessive way that made him feel small and mean.


But more than that, he hated himself. For sitting like a good little royal while she leaned into the space that supposed to be his. The space he wanted to be his. The space he missed every night Mydeimos was gone.


And Mydeimos hadn’t even looked at him, not even a glance. His eyes remaine calm. Expression unreadable as he let her linger in the circle of his light like it wasn’t burning someone else alive in the corner.


Somehow, it made him feel worsen.


Ten minutes. Ten, agonizing, teeth-gritting minutes.


That’s how long Phainon sat there. Limbs stiff, smile frozen, pretending not to notice every flick of Cifera’s fingers, every lean, every smile she shot at Mydeimos like they were sharing a private language only the two of them knew. His eyes counted the seconds on the grandfather clock while his heart pounded in an uneven rhythm in his ears. A minute felt like ten. Ten felt like a lifetime.


Finally, Cifera straightened, rolled up the scrolls on the desk, and gave Mydeimos a teasing little smirk.


“Don’t forget,” she said. “Tomorrow, same time?”


Mydeimos gave a noncommittal nod, eyes still skimming the documents. “Tell the seamstress I’ll stop by after the council meeting.”


“Of course,” she purred. Then she turned her gaze on Phainon. Her smile curled upward like a blade wrapped in velvet.


“It was nice finally meeting you, Queen,” she said, lilting, perfectly polite.


Phainon gave her a smile in return—tight, shallow, empty. He said nothing as she glided out of the room.


The door clicked shut behind her.


Then the silece came back.


Mydeimos was seated at his desk, sleeves rolled to his elbows, pale fingers stained with ink as he penned some decree or correspondence. He didn’t even glance up.


Phainon sat still for a minute longer, the air in his lungs starting to itch.


Waiting.


It wasn’t new. He had become familiar with the stillness. With the weight of his own silence, the ticking of the clock, the sound of the quill.


He wasn’t angry, no. He didn’t even know if he had the right to be.


He hadn’t expected a banquet. Not a parade, not even a shared bed. He didn’t care for grand weddings or whispered prayers to the Titans. He didn’t need anyone to bow or cheer.


He hadn’t asked for anything.


But he had hoped, at least, that there would be something small. A shared meal. A smile. A glance. A hand held in quiet understanding. Maybe even just one day where Mydeimos looked at him and remembered Phainon was there for him.


But ever since their return to Kremnos, Phainon had been left in the quiet.


Every morning, he woke in a bed too cold, too wide. No note. No word. They didn't even see each other's shadow. Hadn’t touched him beyond that one moment in the carriage, that one kiss that lingered in his bones like a fading bruise. He only had the news passed along by a knight: “His Majesty has left for the northern wall.” “His Majesty is holding court today.” “His Majesty will return by dusk.”


Dusk passed. The hallways darkened. Phainon ate alone again.


He’d grown used to the way the palace seemed to murmur about Mydeimos more than the man himself did. Whispers from passing staff, secondhand words from guards, like he was the only one in the castle who had to guess where his husband might be.


He didn’t want to demand more. He didn’t want to be seen as needy or childish. But something inside him had begun to wilt. Slowly. Without anyone noticing.


And by now, Phainon wasn’t sure what stung more: that Mydeimos hadn’t come to see him or that he told himself to stop expecting anything from his husband-on-paper. 


Phainon heaved a sigh, slowly rearraging his disoriented feeling.


And before he could, Mydeimos finally break the silence, “I heard you were badly hurt after the sparring match.”


Phainon laughed, breathless. “You're two weeks late,” he said. “I’m already healed.”


His voice was light, too light, but it carried the hollow sound of glass about to crack.


"...I see. I'm glad you're recovered well."


And that was his only response. Another silence engulfed them, broken only by the dry rasp of parchment, the scratch of Mydeimos’s quill, and the occasional rustle of fabric when he adjusted the papers on his desk.


Phainon didn't speak ether. He couldn’t. The words sat like iron in his throat.


He hated how his eyes kept drifting to the desk. Hated how his hands clenched into fists in his lap. Hated how the room suddenly felt too small for his chest and yet too wide, like Mydeimos was miles away even though they shared the same air.


He shouldn’t feel this way.


He really shouldn’t.


But the ache didn’t stop just because he wanted it to end. It throbbed low in his ribs, sharp like rejection, bitter. Phainon thought he was used to wait, he spent more than a decade for Mydeimos. But this was much harder than that, even though they actually had something now.


He looked down at his hands. No rings. Of course not. Kremnos didn’t put much weight in wedding bands. Now, he started to question everything again. He couldn't help wondering if Mydeimos ever thought of him when he was gone, buried under court work, council meetings, border disputes, whatever else seemed to matter more than showing up in front of his own husband.


( Was everything just in my head? )


( Now to think about it, I don't even know about his feeling... )


( Mydeimos did said he wanted a divorce later, I was the one who rejected it. )


( He seems fine on his own... )


( And I was the one who forced this relationship...)


( What if I'm not actually needed here...? )

Phainon heaved a deep breath but it didn't seem to lift the lump on his throat. He didn’t want to be here anymore. Didn’t want to cling on the thought that he held any importance.

( Hahah, all that talks about bringing him peace... )


( I'm so full of myself, huh... )


( ...Maybe, I should've chose to get imprisoned, haha. )


Phainon slowly stood up, running a palm to brush his hair back.


“I’ll go back to my room,” he said, too smooth, like a blade drawn slow from its sheath. “You’ve got work to do.”


He didn't wait for answer to reach the door. It wasn’t dramatic. No stomping. No doors slammed open. Just quiet footsteps.


Mydeimos froze. His eyes snapped up. The quill dropped, clattering against the wood.


“Wait—” he stood up, the pitch he used was lower than usual, tensed even. “I’m not done talking.”


Phainon didn’t stop.


“Phainon,” Mydeimos said behind him, quiet.


Phainon didn’t stop.


“Phainon,” louder now, more insistent.


Still, he walked.


And then—


“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”


It was the voice of a king.


And it stopped him cold.


His feet locked to the marble floor. His back stiffened. The breath caught in his chest as if the words themselves had wrapped around his spine and pulled tight. He then turned slowly, calmly. His face showed nothing, but his chest felt like it was caving in.


Mydeimos stood a few steps behind, taller in posture now, shoulders squared. The weight of his title pressed into the space between them.


“Yes, Your Majesty?” he asked gently.


The honorific was a knife.


Mydeimos frowned. “What are you angry for?”


“I’m not angry,” Phainon replied.


“You’re walking away.”


“I am,” he agreed, still smiling, still painfully polite. “But not out of anger.”


“Then why?”


Phainon hesitated. The smile slipped.


“Well, I just don't know what else I should do,” he said softly. “So, I'll just do what I did lately. Waiting. In the room you prepared for me. That's the best I can do for you, right? Waiting.”


“Phainon, I apologise,” Mydeimos said, quieter now. “For being absent. For the silence. I’ve been—”


“Busy?” Phainon finished for him, his tone was neutral but his smile grew weaker. “Of course you are busy. You’re the king. I know my place.”


Mydeimos’s eyes narrowed, brows drawing low. “That’s not what I meant. I...”


"I'm tired, Mydei."


Phainon looked down, laughed under his breath, quiet and humorless.


“I’m tired of waiting without knowing what I’m waiting for. Tired of rooms that echo. Tired of meals eaten alone. Tired of sleeping in a bed that too big for me alone. It feels like I married this castle instead of you.”


Mydeimos flinched, but Phainon held up a hand before he could speak.


“I’m not blaming you,” he said softly. “I know you’re busy. I know you have a country to rule. I understand, I really do. I just…I thought… maybe, I wouldn’t be forgotten no matter how busy you are...”


His voice cracked a little. He hated that.


“I’m not angry at you, really,” he repeated. “I just feel… so stupid. For waiting like a fool in a room you never walk into. For not knowing anything. For feeling like I’m the only one who didn’t get the memo. For not knowing what am I even doing here.”


He laughed again, bitterly.


“I don’t even know where you will you go tomorrow. You won't tell me, right? I guess you'll just let the answer come from someone else’s mouth than yours. And I will just wait again, until you have time to talk to me directly than to the guard in front of my door.”


"Phainon," Mydeimos took a step closer. “I never meant to make you feel that way.”


“I know,” Phainon said. “That’s what makes it worse.”


Phainon breathed through his mouth, his eyes felt so heavy that he had to bat his eyelashes fast to calm his lacrimal gland from shedding anything.


Mydeimos glanced away once and he took a step forward, closer to Phainon. His hand, still smelled like ink, was held out, waiting to be completed.


“Phainon, let's sit down and talk it out,” Mydeimos softly pleaded, his golden eyes dimmed under the moonlight. “Please.”


But Phainon just shook his head, shut his eyes from his sight.


“I need to breathe,” he whispered. “And if I stay here, I’ll say something I’ll regret.”


He bowed slightly, formally, before he walked towards his room.


This time, Mydeimos didn't chase after him. The king looked at his own empty hand clenched it, feeling the coldness of something absent. It always cold, aching, but it felt like a deep stab into his heart now.


"...I messed up." He whispered to no one but the crescent mark that his nail left on the palm. 

**

The council chamber was quiet, too quiet for a room that held six of Kremnos’ most prominent men.


Mydeimos sat at the head of the long stone table, fingers pressed lightly together beneath his chin, golden gaze distant. Papers lay before him: border reports, tax ledgers, and correspondence from distant provinces but he hadn’t flipped a single one in minutes.


At his right sat Hephaestion, draped in his usual loose black tunic, long blond hair pulled into a lazy tail that somehow made him look even more boyish than he already did. He tapped his fingers idly on the table, glancing between the others.


“Do we continue talking about the valley harvest,” Hephaestion finally drawled, “or should we just start composing a tragedy titled ‘The Distracted King and His Endless Stare Into the Void’?”


Perdikkas exhaled a quiet chuckle from across the table, seated with his legs crossed and a medicinal pouch hanging from his hip. The royal physician twirled a thin strand of rosemary between his fingers, watching Mydeimos as one might watch a brewing fever.


Leonnius, always stiff with discipline, cleared his throat. “Your Majesty,” he said carefully, “you haven’t responded to the northern dispatch.”


Ptolemy looked up from his tome, one of his many self-authored chronicles on Mydeimos, and murmured, “‘A warlord who loses focus shall find his battlefield already lost.’ I think I wrote that in Chapter Four.”


Hephaestion groaned and reached over to smack the back of his head. “Stop quoting yourself.”


“I am a published strategist,” Ptolemy replied primly, smoothing the page.


In the far corner, Peucesta sat with a half-tuned lyre in his lap. He didn’t speak, he rarely did, but his head tilted ever so slightly toward Mydeimos, gaze unreadable, as though he could already hear the dissonance in his king’s rhythm.


The silence intruded the meeting.


And Mydeimos still hadn’t moved.


Hephaestion leaned forward, resting his chin on one palm. “All right. Enough. What was it this time? Was it the goat milk? Did the kitchen run out?”


That earned him a side-glare from the king, mild but sharp enough to sting. “It’s not the goat milk,” Mydeimos said, finally. His voice was quiet, worn-out.


“So there is something.” Hephaestion grinned, but it faded as Mydeimos rubbed his temple, posture sagging just enough to be human.


“We should focus.”


“We are,” Perdikkas said, gently. “But if our king is half-present, then none of this matters. A sick body cannot lead.”


“It’s nothing...” Mydeimos started.


“It’s the queen, isn’t it?” Leonnius blurted, then immediately looked like he regretted it.


The entire table turned to him.


Leonnius adjusted his gloves nervously. “I, I was just returning from the west tower. There were whispers from the sentries near the upper hall. Fret not, I halted them. No word will leave the palace.”


Peucesta gave a small nod of approval. Ptolemy scribbled something in the margins of his book.


“‘Even shadows speak if not silenced.’” He read aloud, pleased.


Mydeimos leaned back in his chair, hand over his mouth.


He had never intended for that moment with Phainon to be public, let alone scandalous. But the quiet tension in the hallway must’ve wrapped around them like thread, noticeable to even the passing guard.


And Phainon’s voice, when he referred Mydeimos as Your Majesty, that had cut deeper than any dagger.


Hephaestion’s expression softened. “You fought?”


“Not really.” Mydeimos exhaled. “I didn’t speak enough to call it a fight.”


“Then what was it?” Perdikkas raised the question gently.


Mydeimos bit his lower lip, gaze was focused on his own thumb like it was something worth scrutinizing.


“Phainon... My husband feels like a stranger in this castle.”


None of them spoke. The words lingered, stark and cold.


“I didn’t give him a ceremony,” Mydeimos went on, bitter. “I didn’t give him a shared chamber. I married him by decree, then vanished into war meetings and trade councils. He eats alone. Sleeps alone. And he finds out about me from the mouths of knights, not from me.”


He rubbed his hands together slowly. “And the worst part is… I didn’t mean to hurt him. I simply kept doing what I thought I had to. For the kingdom. For order. For his safety.”


“Mydeimos, you did not wed a title,” Ptolemy murmured. “You wed a person.”


“I know,” Mydeimos muttered.


Hephaestion leaned back in his chair, arms crossed. “So… what are you going to do?”


Mydeimos looked up.


“I don’t know,” he admitted. “I’ve led armies. I’ve killed my own blood. I can stare down a thousand soldiers and not blink but his silence scares me.”


He closed his eyes, and this time, even Peucesta looked away, respectfully.


“I thought… maybe he’d understand. That he’d keep waiting until I fixed everything else. I expected him to always welcome me with his smile.”


He opened his eyes.


“But he said he’s not angry. That’s the worst part. He’s just… tired. And I don’t know how to reach him anymore.”

The heavy air of the war chamber hadn’t lifted, even after Mydeimos’ quiet admission.


He sat hunched slightly forward, golden eyes fixed somewhere on the cold marble floor, as if the silence could give him an answer. Across the table, his trusted aides exchanged glances, some wary, others understanding. None of them were used to seeing their king so uncertain.


“So?” Hephaestion broke the silence, arms crossed loosely as he leaned back in his chair. “What's the plan? You’ve identified the problem. What's next, oh wise king?”


Mydeimos exhaled. “I don’t know. I'm still thinking.”


"And it's like, how many days passed?"

"Two..."

Hephaestion clicked his tongue. “You’re lucky our Queen is very persistent. Anyone else would’ve already packed up and left. Or punched you. Probably both.”


“Definitely both,” Perdikkas murmured, folding his arms.


Leonnius stepped forward, brow furrowed with worry. “My king, if I may… Your Majesty has always carried burdens alone. But this is different. You are no longer just a ruler. You are someone’s partner. You can’t rule him like your kingdom.”


Mydeimos looked up. “I never meant to.”


“I know,” Leonnius said softly. “But did you ever tell him that?”


Mydeimos opened his mouth, then shut it.


Ptolemy, who had been writing quietly at the corner of the table, looked up and added, “‘The storm believes it whispers, until it sees the ruin it leaves behind.’ You may not have meant to hurt him, but neglect, even unintentional, is still a blade.”


“I didn’t neglect him,” Mydeimos muttered.


“Then where were you all these times?” Hephaestion asked. “No ceremony. No banquet. You sent him to the west wing and went straight to council.”


“I had to review the security alert from the border...”


“Your husband didn’t marry the border." Hephaestion interrupted, almost snarky. "Mydeimos, did you forget you practically ripped him away from his family by force? He's all alone in this foreign land. And you, from all people, should've understood how that feel like.”


That silenced the room again.


Peucesta, who had been quietly plucking a single string on his lyre without sound, finally looked up.


His voice, as always, was soft and deliberate. “My King, what do you feel… about the queen?”


Mydeimos blinked at him.


Peucesta tilted his head. “You speak about him as though you carry the weight of the world. But I’ve never heard you say it. So, tell us. What is it you feel?”


A pause.


Then Mydeimos straightened in his chair and, without flinching, said:


“I love him.”


The words echoed sharply in the cold chamber. Hephaestion had a deadpan expression. Perdikkas coughed. Leonnius looked like he wasn’t sure if he was allowed to smile. Ptolemy muttered, “Chapter Ten, confirmed,” and furiously scratched something down.


Peucesta smirked, shaking his head with that rare glimmer of amusement.


“I love him,” Mydeimos repeated. “I love him so much, it terrifies me. I think about him constantly. When he smiles, I forget how to speak. When he sulks, I want to throw my crown off a cliff. When he’s angry, I feel like I deserve death penalty.” He huffed, looking away, ears faintly red. "But every time I saw him waiting for me in the corridor, in the garden, in the room I made too far from mine, I just… I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t know what to say. It felt like my head just turned into one big jumbled mess.”


Hephaestion scoffed. “Mydeimos, you absolute idiot romantic.”


“I am an idiot,” Mydeimos muttered.


He stared at the empty spot of the table before him. “Because I don’t know how to love.”


No one interrupted.


“I was raised to be a weapon. Then I became a fugitive. Then I became a king. And I’ve never had time to be anything in between.
