No one was to disturb the royal suite.

Not that anyone wanted to.

Because while no one truly knew what happened inside, it wasn’t hard to guess. Not with the muffled thumps echoing through the stone walls. Not with the strange, breathy sounds that came and went, sweet and low and too intimate to be mistaken. The servants pretended to be deaf. The knights developed a sudden fascination with the floor tiles.

Rumors, naturally, ran rampant.

“They must be fighting passionately.”

“Did you hear that crash last night? Something broke. Sounded like a table.”

"Bless the Queen. I hope he survived the ordeal. Marrying our King is not easy."

Still, no one dared approach the door.

When it finally opened on the morning of the third day, the change was instant.

The king and the queen didn’t say a word, simply walked out side by side, calm, composed, hands faintly brushing. Their shared gaze made it clear: whatever storm had raged inside that room had passed.

But the changes didn’t stop there.

The queen never returned to his old chambers. From then on, only one room bore both of their coats-of-arms above the arch. The servants were stunned speechless the first morning Phainon appeared at the king’s breakfast table in his private chamber, yawning, hair a mess, clad in one of Mydeimos’s dark robes. Mydeimos had the gall to act as if it were normal, slicing bread for two, pouring pomegranate juice with goat milk without looking up.

Meals were always taken together now. Sometimes, they even cooked for each other though this often resulted in a dozen panicked maids trying to salvage a kitchen under siege by two royals.

But what made people smiled that they were seen together.

A lot.

Not just in war councils or royal decrees, but in the quiet spaces in between. Phainon appeared in the gardens with Mydeimos, laughing with stained fingers as they attempted to prune a lemon tree. Mydeimos was spotted leaning over a market stall, letting Phainon feed him a piece of honeyed fig. They walked together to attend a banquet, sat too close on the same bench during court, whispered during ceremonies as if the entire kingdom weren’t watching their every move.

And they were seen at least once in three days at the most 'romantic' space: the training ground.

That day too, the hall rang with sharp exhales, low grunts, and the distinct crack of wood breaking. Somewhere in the chaos, a rack of training swords toppled over with a crash that made one of the guards outside flinch.

Inside, it was war.

At least, it looked like it.

Mydeimos moved like a storm, controlled, calculated, his golden eyes focused with deadly intent. Phainon, on the other hand, was a whirlwind of unpredictable strikes and impossible agility, laughing between breathless bursts of motion.

Phainon spat a streak of blood onto the ground, wiping his mouth with the back of his hand as he circled around Mydeimos. “That was a cheap shot.”

“You left your guard open,” Mydeimos said flatly, rolling his left shoulder with a crack. His golden eyes flicked down Phainon’s body. “And you’re sloppy today.”

“I’m not sloppy.” Phainon grinned. “Just distracted. You look hot when you’re being ruthless.”

“Focus, Phainon.”

“You're my main focus.”

And he lunged.

Their bodies clashed midair, a collision of heat, sweat, and sharp intent. Phainon twisted, hooking an arm under Mydeimos’s elbow, trying to drag him into a lock, but Mydeimos moved with swift precision, flipping over and landing a solid knee into Phainon’s stomach. Phainon gasped, folded but before he could fall, he kicked up, catching Mydeimos in the thigh.

The king grunted.

The world blurred.

This was how they communicate, flirting with fists. But still, they weren’t holding back. The kind of fight that would leave marks for days—purple, red between the traces of their love-making.

And they loved it.

“Come on, sunshine,” Mydeimos taunted, ducking as Phainon’s fist narrowly missed his cheek. “That all you’ve got?”

Phainon, panting, grinned. “You're so beautiful when you're trying to break my bones.”

He got a punch to the jaw in return. It snapped his head to the side. He stumbled but when he turned back, he was laughing, chest heaving.

Mydeimos didn’t smile, but something glinted in his eyes.

They went again.

The hall rang with impact after impact. Elbow to ribs, foot to shin, palm against temple. Blood was smeared across Phainon’s cheek, a thin cut above his brow painting down like warpaint. Mydeimos had his lip split, his hair messy and stuck to his temple with sweat. They were panting, glaring, eyes blown wide not just with exertion but something darker, more dangerous. Admiration. Obsession.

“Remind me—” Mydeimos spun, sweeping Phainon's legs with his own in a blur, “—what part of this was relaxing?”

Phainon yelped as he went down hard, the air punched from his lungs, body hitting the hard ground with a heavy thud.

But instead of groaning in pain, he let out a breathless laugh. Because Mydeimos had straddled his hips to pin him, one hand gripping his collar, the other still pressed against his chest. And Phainon, wild-eyed and grinning like a man absolutely not taking things seriously, blinked up and said: “Wow.”

Mydeimos narrowed his eyes. “What?”

“You look really good from this angle.”

“…Phainon.”

“I mean, you always look good, but like, woah. The king, just pinning me down, drenched in sweat and fury? You could end me, and I’d say thank you.”

Mydeimos’s expression shifted somewhere between exasperation and flushed. “Can you stop that?”

Phainon just wiggled slightly under him and grinned wider. “You say that, but you like seeing me being helpless, don't you?”

Mydeimos pushed off with a low sigh, standing and brushing hair from his face. “I’ll bruise you for real.”

“I’d wear it like jewelry.”

“You're such a pervert."

Phainon let out a low groan and stared at his husband like he was a living miracle.

“…You don’t get it,” Phainon panted. “You pin me down like this, breathing like that, glaring like that… how do you not expect me to fall in love all over again?”

Mydeimos wiped blood from his lip with the back of his hand. “You’re a lunatic.”

“It takes one to know one.”

Mydeimos pressed a thumb against protrusion of Phainon's neck. Not hard, just enough to make a threat.

Yet, Phainon just laughed, whispered, “You gonna keep doing that? ‘Cause I’m not complaining even if you wrap all of your pretty fingers around my neck. Like you did last night when I hit too deep.”

“Shut up,” Mydeimos muttered.

Phainon grinned as he lay sprawled out on the floor, limbs aching, head spinning, heart full. “Make me.”

Mydeimos pulled the choker on Phainon's neck upward as he leaned down, sealed the words with his own lips.

Their lips were bruised, cut in places. The taste of iron mixed with something sweet. Phainon’s honeyed breath, the faint tang of pomegranate, sweat, and blood. It should’ve hurt, and it did, but it only added the taste they both happened to get adrenaline from.

Phainon made a soft sound, a catch in his throat. His hand gripped Mydeimos' nape, not pulling away but pulling him closer. Their mouths moved with an aching hunger, not lust, not yet, but like they needed to feel alive, to remember they were alive, together.

Mydeimos exhaled hard against Phainon’s lips, trembling slightly.

“You’re bleeding again,” Phainon murmured.

“So are you,” Mydeimos whispered back. His thumb grazed the edge of Phainon’s jaw, smearing the blood like a rouge to Phainon's lips.

Phainon chuckled breathlessly, their foreheads touching now, sweat slicked between them. Then their lips brushed again, slower this time. Less defiant, more desperate. Mydeimos rested his hand over Phainon’s chest where his heart thudded wildly beneath bruising ribs and love-struck foolishness.

Among the wreckage of wooden benches, broken dummies, and discarded weapons, the king and his husband shared their affection, again and again.

Battered, bruised, bloodstained, and more in love than ever.

Mydeimos had called his trusted friends to the chamber usually reserved for internal military briefings. The walls were lined with scroll racks and Kremnoan banners. A warm draft filtered through the tall windows, sunlight catching dust in the air like golden flecks.


Hephaestion, Ptolemy, Leonnius, Perdikkas, and Peucesta entered one by one.


And then they saw it.


Their king sat at the head of the long table, uncharacteristically relaxed in a modest, slate-blue tunic that covered his entire torso. Covered. Not a single glimpse of his usual ceremonial chest-wrap, nor the ever-present metal threads tracing his arms. His golden-red hair was partially unbound.


More shocking still: behind him, Phainon stood on a stepstool, carefully combing Mydeimos’s hair and braiding sections of it with practiced fingers, humming something suspiciously cheerful under his breath.


And Mydeimos? The infamous war-scarred monarch of Kremnos, a man known for turning assassins to corpse with a flick of his gaze?


Was sitting obediently. Patiently. Letting it happen.


The five men froze in the doorway like birds caught mid-flight.


“…You’re early,” Mydeimos said, without looking up.


“My apologies, Your Majesty,” Hephaestion said automatically, then paused as Phainon reached forward to adjust one of the hairpieces. “Er, should we come back later?”


“No,” Mydeimos said, waving a hand. “You’re fine. Sit.”


They all sat.


Awkwardly.


Peucesta blinked and tilted his head ever so slightly. Perdikkas rubbed his temple like a man preparing for war. Ptolemy fumbled with a book he wasn’t even reading. Leonnius stared directly at the corner of the table, as if it held all the answers in the universe.


Hephaestion, bravest among them, cleared his throat. “Your Majesty… was there something urgent you wished to discuss?”


“Yes,” Mydeimos said. “I gathered you to thank you. For reminding me what I was about to lose. For giving me the courage to stop running.”


There was a pause.


Then murmurs of “It was nothing,” and “We merely said the truth,” rose from the table. Hephaestion shrugged, scratching his jaw. “Well, someone had to tell you. You’ve been sulking like an ancient sculpture.”


“I do not sulk,” Mydeimos replied evenly.


Phainon muffled a chuckle.


The five exchanged glances.


Phainon, still braiding, though the braid had turned a little lopsided, seemed not to notice the growing discomfort in the room. Or he noticed, and chose not to care. He tugged gently at Mydeimos’s hair, then leaned in closer.


“Almost done,” he murmured, grinning.


“You’ve said that three times now,” Mydeimos said dryly, but didn’t move away.


The five looked at each other again. Because they noticed.


The bruises.


Faint but visible, some on Phainon’s collarbone and upper arm, a few on his jaw, already darkening into blue-purple hues. Mydeimos, while mostly covered for once, had a cut at the edge of his lip and something that looked like it might be a particularly sharp-angled hickey just above his collar. They looked… mildly destroyed.


Ptolemy mouthed to Hephaestion: "Did they fight again?"


Hephaestion mouthed back: "Or something else."


Leonnius was visibly sweating. Peucesta plucked at the strings of an invisible lyre in his mind and looked deeply, deeply conflicted.


Perdikkas’s mouth twitched. “Should we be concerned?”


Mydeimos finally turned, his expression composed. “We're fine. We just sparred.”


They all nodded very slowly, all five heads moving in unison.


“Of course.”


“Right.”


“Just sparring.”


“Very passionate sparring.”


Mydeimos narrowed his eyes.


Phainon, still blissfully cheerful, leaned over his shoulder. “We just sparred, honest. We broke the weapon rack.”


“A, ah. We heard that,” Leonnius muttered. "The young knights were concerned. They thought you two were about to kill each other.”


“Ah, yeah,” Phainon nodded.  “We did try. It was exhilarating. You should’ve seen how he threw me across the room. There’s a dent in the wall now.”


Peucesta blinked slowly, hands folded in his lap. “And that’s… good?”


“Oh, yeah.” Phainon grinned. “I think I might’ve fallen in love all over again. My husband is feral. He kissed all the pain away too.”


Silence.


Ptolemy dropped his book. Peucesta coughed into his hand. Perdikkas looked like he was running trauma calculations. Hephaestion was trying, very visibly, not to cringe.


But all of them were having the same thoughts that Phainon thought and acted like a real Kremnoan than any of them.


Meanwhile, Mydeimos tilted his head toward Phainon. “Sit down before you give them more to question.”


Phainon plopped into the seat beside him with the ease of a man who believed himself bulletproof.


Their hands found each other on the table, fingers naturally lacing together.


Mydeimos looked at them again, his closest circle, those who had weathered fire and storm and grief beside him.


“I owe you more than I can express,” he said simply. “This kingdom stands because of your loyalty. And now I stand, more myself than I’ve been in years, because you reminded me I’m not alone.”


Ptolemy sniffled. “That one’s going in the book.”


Leonnius finally smiled.


Hephaestion rolled his eyes but didn’t hide the grin.


Peucesta raised an eyebrow, silently proud.


The meeting resumed, well, tried to.


After the awkward yet weirdly heartwarming display of affection between the king and his now emotionally-resurrected consort, the five advisors did their best to rearrange their composure and open their tomes, notes, and scrolls.


Perdikkas cleared his throat. “That said, Your Majesty, now that the palace has… resumed domestic equilibrium… perhaps it’s time to address a more longstanding matter.”


Mydeimos didn’t even lift his head. “What is it?”


Hephaestion answered dryly, “The matter of an heir.”


Phainon blinked, mid-reach for a grape from the plate beside Mydeimos. “Huh?”


Ptolemy interjected helpfully, “Succession. The royal line. Continuity of the crown, should something happen.”


Leonnius raised a careful hand. “To be clear, none of us are wishing doom on either of you. But the topic will come up. Especially after the…uh, state of your return to the public eye.”


Mydeimos glanced at Phainon, who was still chewing a grape.


“I don’t need an heir,” he said plainly.


The five exchanged glances.


“Nor will I take a second consort,” he added flatly.


Peucesta nodded once in silent agreement.


But Leonnius, ever cautious, gently added, “It’s not about another partner. We have that method, Your Majesty. The old Kremnoan rite. It’s been used before. Rarely, but successfully… to allow male-consorts to conceive. You’d both still remain bonded to one another.”


“It’s very dangerous,” Perdikkas interrupted, fingers steepled under his chin. “Even among pure-blooded Kremnoans, the rite draws on body and core alike. It was designed with our physiology in mind. Blood-forged through generations. Using it on anyone outside that lineage would be… reckless.”


Phainon’s eyes narrowed, playful spark glinting in cyan.


“Right. Reckless but I think you guys are looking at the wrong place.” he said, standing and slowly circling behind Mydeimos now, his hands trailing lightly down the king’s broad shoulders before stopping just beneath his jaw. “I’m not the one who’d be carrying.”


He tilted Mydeimos’s chin upward gently. Mydeimos’s golden eyes widened ever so slightly, locking with his.


“So, I think the real question here,” Phainon murmured, the tune of his words dropping to something silkier, deeper, each syllable touched with that commanding edge he rarely used, “is whether you would bear my child, my king.”


The chamber went still.


Hephaestion's pen dropped. Ptolemy fumbled his book. Leonnius made a noise that might have been a strangled cough. Even the ever-silent Peucesta turned his gaze up, wide-eyed for once.


But the most astonishing thing was the subtle shift in Mydeimos.


A faint twitch of his brow, his breath hitching audibly, a sharp contrast to his usual stillness. A flush spread, profoundly, down the side of his neck, visible even beneath the high collar of his robe.


He didn’t pull away from Phainon’s touch. In fact… he leaned into it, gaze half-lidded, breath shallow.


Mydeimos. The king. The scourge of Castrum Kremnos. The man who once ripped a warlord’s head off with one hand and gave a speech the same night was now blushing so deeply it reached the tips of his ears.


All five advisors were now at varying stages of spiritual exit. Perdikkas looked like he aged ten years. Hephaestion was staring into the void. Peucesta, by some divine will, hadn’t blinked in thirty seconds. Leonnius was quietly chewing his tongue. Ptolemy was muttering something under his breath about “scandalous epics” and “should I write it down or not”.


Phainon's lopsided smile stretched, like he thrived in the chaos he left behind. He gently pressed a kiss to Mydeimos’s temple, adding a saccharine, “Well?”


And Mydeimos did not deny it.


He only muttered, low and sharp, “...Let's discuss it in private.”


Which, everyone could see, meant a pending yes.


Hephaestion stood abruptly. “I believe this meeting has reached a natural end.”


“I second that,” Ptolemy said, already gathering his scattered pages like a man fleeing a battlefield.


Leonnius muttered something about patrol schedules. Peucesta gave a short nod and made for the door in silence. Perdikkas looked genuinely traumatised by reality.


The aides scrambled to adjourn the meeting faster than any war briefing they’d ever delivered. Chairs scraped, books were snapped shut, and a series of mumbled excuses echoed like a retreating army. No one had enough bravery to witness what was about to follow.


Thus, the door shut with a final, echoing clack.


And then there were two.


Phainon leaned back in his chair with a satisfied sigh. “Well, that went well.”


Mydeimos stared at the ceiling, contemplating many things, like why he loved and married this man, and why he had no regrets about it after everything.


“You need to tone it down,” Mydeimos muttered, dry as sand.


Phainon leaned back with a chuckle, crossing his arms behind his head. “Oh, come on. They needed the entertainment. Did you see Perdikkas? He looked like he was going to combust.”


“You're breaking him.”


“I'm not! Sooner or later, they gotta know how cute their king is.”


Mydeimos sighed through his nose, but there was no heat behind it. His gaze wandered for a moment, then dropped quietly to the floor.


Then, almost too softly, Mydeimos asked, “Would you ever want… a child?”


Phainon blinked.


He took a moment, not because he didn’t know the answer, but because the gravity in Mydeimos’s voice needed something more than instinctive honesty. Still, he smiled, softer this time.


“I won’t lie,” he said. “I would. Someday. But only if it’s safe… and only if you want it too.”


Mydeimos’s gaze lingered on the stone floor, his fingers idly tracing the hem of his sleeve. 

“…I do want to,” he admitted. “Sometimes I imagine what it’d be like. Holding something that’s a part of you. A part of me. Watching them grow...”


He trailed off, his brow furrowing.


“But it's, a little bit terrifying..”


Phainon tilted his head.


“You know me. I'm not the best in being gentle,” Mydeimos said. “And, looking at my father... I’m… not certain I’d be any different. My father wasn't always like what the world remember. What if, I turned mad? Or maybe I will stay sane but what if I'm not what they wanted as a father...?”


There was pain in his voice, not loud but cold, old, curled around his ribs and stayed there.


Phainon reached out, gently taking his hand.


“You’re not him,” he said. “You’ve never been him. You are more powerful but you wield it better than him. I mean, you can always continue his legacy but you chose differently. Slowly but sure, things gradually changed.”


Mydeimos glanced at him, doubt flickering behind golden eyes.


“And even if you do mess up,” Phainon added, “you’re not doing this alone. You have me. And I’ll be there every step of the way. I’ll read all the scrolls, brew all the weird Kremnoan prenatal drinks, fight off the nightmares, whatever it takes.”


He smiled, pressing Mydeimos’s hand to his chest where his heart thudded, warm and steady.


“I want to raise a child with you, Mydei. Not just to have one.”


Mydeimos exhaled, a little less heavy than before. He nodded once, slowly.


“Alright. This is not only about us. We'll need to think about it thoroughly.” he murmured.


"Yeah. Let's take it easy." Phainon grinned. “Though, remember that anytime you’re ready to bear my child, just say it. I'll do my best to fill you up.”


Mydeimos gave him a look of pure disbelief, half-exasperated, half-flustered. “Why do you say things like that so casually?”


Phainon winked. “Because I like watching you suffer.”


Mydeimos rolled his eyes. But when Phainon leaned in to brush their foreheads together, he didn’t pull away.


And so, Kremnos began to change.


Not with the clash of swords, but with softer things. The once-crimson halls learned to hold laughter, and the throne, long used to solitude, grew used to the echo of two sets of footstep, Where once the king stood alone, now he stood with a bright-smiled consort who refused to be left behind. Mydeimos, once feared as an immortal tyrant, learned to pause, for quiet moments, for the warmth of a hand always reaching back. Phainon, whose smile once belonged to the mundane farm life, now belonged to the chaotic Kremnos too. 


And in the hush between festivals and war councils, the quietest rumor fluttered through the streets: of the palace light burning late, of another fistfight which ended with kisses and perhaps—just perhaps—of a new heartbeat would soon join the rhythm of the realm.
